paragraphs.text: Organic–inorganic halide perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have emerged as one of the most promising photovoltaic technologies, driven by their rapid increase in power conversion efficiency (PCE) and compatibility with low-cost solution processing [1,2]. The archetypal perovskite absorber adopts the general formula ABX3, where A is an organic cation, B is a divalent metal cation, and X is a halide anion [3]. Among these, methylammonium lead triiodide (MAPbI3, MA+ = CH3NH3+) has been extensively studied due to its favorable tetragonal phase at room temperature, strong visible-light absorption, long carrier diffusion lengths, and suitable bandgap for single-junction photovoltaic architectures [4]. As a result, single-junction PSCs have achieved certified PCEs of up to 26.1%, positioning them as competitive alternatives to conventional silicon-based solar cells [5].

The outstanding efficiencies of PSCs are rooted in several intrinsic advantages of the perovskite absorber: large absorption coefficients, high charge-carrier mobilities, weakly bound excitons that readily dissociate into free carriers, and long minority carrier diffusion lengths [6]. However, these benefits are severely compromised by structural imperfections that arise during film formation. MAPbI3 films typically contain a range of defects including undercoordinated halide ions, undercoordinated Pb2+ centers, Pb clusters, Pb–I antisite defects (PbI3), and vacancies of I− or MA+, which act as non-radiative recombination centers and accelerate degradation [7,8,9]. In polycrystalline films, small grain sizes and high densities of grain boundaries exacerbate recombination losses, impede charge transport, and ultimately limit both PCE and operational stability [10]. Importantly, the density and distribution of these defects are closely linked to the nucleation and crystal-growth dynamics during solution processing [11]. The rapid and often uncontrolled crystallization of MAPbI3 from precursor solutions tends to generate heterogeneous nucleation, mosaic domains, and abundant grain boundaries [12]. These microstructural flaws degrade optoelectronic quality and facilitate defect migration and ion transport. Under illumination, the photoinduced strain and thermal expansion of the MAPbI3 lattice can further reduce the activation energy for the halide-vacancy migration, thereby further facilitating the ion migration and performance degradation over time [13]. Therefore, the control of the crystallization kinetics and grain growth of perovskite is central to obtaining high-quality films with reduced defect densities, larger grain sizes, and strong operational stability.

To address these challenges, a variety of additive-engineering and interface-modification strategies have been explored. In the precursor solution or at the interfaces, functional small molecules, polymers, ionic liquids and inorganic salts have been incorporated to tune crystallization, passivate defects and stabilize the perovskite phase [14]. A broad range of additives has been investigated to regulate the formation of MAPbI3 films and reduce losses associated with structural and electronic defects. These additives can be broadly grouped according to their chemical nature and function. Lewis-basic compounds, including thiourea, urea, and sulfoxide derivatives, interact with Pb2+ ions in the precursor solution. Such coordination can alter intermediate-phase formation, slow crystallization, and promote the development of larger and more uniform grains [15]. Ammonium and alkylammonium halides are commonly introduced to compensate for halide-related defects and passivate electrically active sites at grain boundaries and interfaces, often resulting in improved open-circuit voltage [16]. Polymers such as polyethylene glycol (PEG), polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP), and poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) can influence nucleation and grain growth while improving film coverage and providing partial protection against moisture. Ionic liquids containing imidazolium or pyridinium cations offer another approach because their low volatility and ionic character allow them to modify precursor properties and interact with charged defects in the perovskite layer [17]. Inorganic salts, particularly alkali-metal halides and pseudohalide compounds, have also been employed to regulate crystallization, passivate defects, and limit ion-migration-related losses [18]. Although these additive families operate through different pathways, they share the objective of improving film quality, reducing non-radiative recombination, and stabilizing device operation. Their development has contributed substantially to the progress of MAPbI3 solar cells, with reported efficiencies increasing from below 15% to more than 21% during the past decade [19].

Despite substantial advances in additive engineering, several persistent limitations continue to restrict the development of broadly applicable molecular design principles. One important issue is the functional specificity of many reported additives. Compounds selected to regulate nucleation and crystal growth do not necessarily passivate the electronic defects remaining in the deposited film [20]. A second limitation concerns the restricted structural tunability of conventional small-molecule additives. Even minor changes to their functional groups or molecular backbones can substantially alter solubility, volatility, thermal stability, and compatibility with the perovskite precursor solution. Consequently, it is difficult to vary one molecular parameter while keeping the remaining physicochemical properties unchanged [21]. Third, practical drawbacks are also associated with several established additive classes. Although ionic liquids can offer strong chemical interactions and favorable processing characteristics, they are often expensive, and poorly immobilized ionic components may contribute to field-driven redistribution and scan-dependent device behavior. Polymeric additives can improve film coverage and mechanical integrity, but excessive incorporation of electrically insulating polymer chains may obstruct charge transport or accumulate at grain boundaries. Similarly, hygroscopic salts, including some lithium- and cesium-containing compounds, can increase the sensitivity of the perovskite layer to ambient moisture and thereby compromise long-term stability [22]. These limitations do not preclude the use of such materials, but they emphasize the need to optimize additive concentration, chemical stability, spatial distribution, and electronic compatibility rather than considering defect passivation alone. Differences in precursor chemistry, deposition conditions, interfacial layers, and measurement protocols further obscure relationships between molecular structure, film formation, defect passivation, and photovoltaic performance. Comparative investigations conducted under otherwise identical conditions are therefore essential for determining which structural features govern additive–precursor interactions and for establishing reliable design rules for multifunctional additives.

Cost and compatibility with scalable manufacturing must also be considered when evaluating the practical relevance of an additive strategy. In many current perovskite solar-cell architectures, the absorber accounts for only a relatively small proportion of the total materials cost, whereas major contributions arise from the hole-transport layer, transparent conducting substrate, and metallic electrode. Accordingly, additives introduced at the low concentrations typically required for crystallization control or defect passivation are unlikely to increase absorber cost substantially. This advantage, however, depends on the use of readily available compounds with simple preparation and purification requirements. Additives that rely on multistep synthesis, specialized reagents, or laborious isolation may offer excellent laboratory-scale performance while remaining unsuitable for large-area production. An effective additive should therefore combine multiple functions, structural tunability, low loading, solution-process compatibility, and economical availability without introducing new pathways for ionic instability, transport losses, or environmental degradation.

While these strategies have led to significant improvements in efficiencies, they frequently lack structural precision and molecular-level tunability. Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) have emerged as highly attractive candidates for rational control of perovskite crystallization and defect chemistry in this regard [23]. COFs are crystalline, porous, organic polymers constructed via strong covalent bonds between predesigned building blocks, giving rise to periodic architectures with well-defined pores and extended π-conjugation [24]. Their low density, large surface area, tunable pore environments, and chemically programmable frameworks make COFs naturally attractive for applications such as photocatalysis, energy storage, and photovoltaics [25]. In perovskite systems in particular, they can play several complementary roles: they provide structural scaffolds that template nucleation and guide crystal growth, they act as electronic modulators that assist charge separation and transport, and they form physical barriers that help to suppress ion migration and protect the material from environmental degradation [26]. For instance, in situ formation of 2D COFs within PbI2 layers has been shown to regulate perovskite crystallization, lower defect densities, and enhance carrier transport. Other studies have demonstrated that carefully chosen COF–perovskite composites can suppress phase degradation (e.g., δ-phase formation in FAPbI3), reduce surface trap states, and significantly improve long-term device stability [27].

Reports on COF–perovskite integration may be categorized according to the location and function of the framework in the device. A frequently studied design is a pre-synthesized COF sandwiched as an interlayer between the perovskite absorber and a charge-transport layer. Lewis-basic groups on the pore surface may interact with undercoordinated Pb2+ sites, minimizing interfacial defects and the accompanying non-radiative recombination in this configuration [28]. For example, Mohamed MG et al. sandwiched two-dimensional Car-ETTA and TFPPy-ETTA COFs between PTAA and the perovskite layer in inverted solar cells [29]. Their porous surfaces promoted perovskite nucleation and crystal growth, resulting in better morphology and crystallinity of the films. The Car-ETTA- and TFPPy-ETTA-based devices gave PCEs of 19.79% and 19.72%, respectively, while the control gave 17.40%. Guo J et al. later utilized sulfhydryl-functionalized COFs (HS-COFs) at both of the perovskite film interfaces [30]. The COF at the buried interface was beneficial in reducing the residual lattice strain and enhancing the resistance to UV exposure, whereas at the top interface, the sulfhydryl groups passivated the surface defects via S–Pb interactions. This dual interface method achieved a PCE of 24.26%, which is one of the highest values recorded for COF-modified perovskite solar cells.

The second technique is to directly introduce COFs into the perovskite absorber as bulk additives. Wu et al. reported a conjugated three-dimensional framework, SP-3D COF, to realize good electrical coupling with the perovskite [31]. The suggested bidirectional charge-transfer process improved carrier transport and enhanced the PCE from 16.70% to 19.07%. Nie et al. improved both film formation and operational stability by using TTDA-TTA COF synthesized from thieno [3,2-b]thiophene-2,5-dicarbaldehyde and 2,4,6-tris(4-aminophenyl)-1,3,5-triazine [32]. The expanded conjugated structure and π–π interactions boosted perovskite crystallization and suppressed degradation in humid and hot settings, achieving a champion PCE of 23.35%. In a similar fashion, Gao X et al. used an amino-functionalized framework (NH2-COF) to control crystallization and passivate defects [15]. The coordination of amino groups and Pb sites enhanced the crystallinity of the film and decreased non-radiative recombination, leading to a champion PCE of 22.13%. These investigations suggest that COFs may enhance perovskite devices by tailoring key interfaces or by regulating crystallization, defect chemistry and charge transport in the absorber.

Two limitations of this body of work motivate the present study. First, the framework is in most cases deposited as a discrete layer or applied as a post-treatment, which retains the process-complexity penalty discussed above and confines the interaction to the surface of the absorber rather than to the grain boundaries distributed throughout it. Reports in which COF chemistry is introduced directly into the MAPbI3 precursor ink, so that it acts during nucleation and growth rather than after it, remain comparatively few. Despite encouraging results, the existing literature provides limited guidance for the rational design of framework modifiers. Individual studies generally focus on only one framework, making it difficult to determine whether the reported improvements arise from linker coordination, pore architecture, π-conjugation, or simply the incorporation of an organic component at grain boundaries [33]. Comparisons among separate reports do not resolve this issue because perovskite-film properties are highly sensitive to experimental variables, including precursor stoichiometry, antisolvent treatment, and annealing conditions, which vary considerably among laboratories [34]. Moreover, many previous investigations have examined compositions other than MAPbI3. These include formamidinium-based absorbers, for which stabilization against the photoinactive δ-phase is a primary concern, and lead-free perovskites studied mainly for photocatalytic applications [35,36]. Because these materials exhibit defect populations and degradation pathways that differ from those of MAPbI3, their reported trends cannot be applied directly to MAPbI3 devices. In particular, there is a lack of comparative studies that investigate how different COF linkers and functional groups regulate MAPbI3 nucleation, grain coalescence, and optoelectronic properties within a unified device platform. Second, almost all published studies examine a single COF system, so the reported improvements cannot be attributed to any particular structural feature of the framework. Without a controlled comparison of chemically distinct frameworks within one device platform, it is not possible to establish which linkage motifs, functional groups, or coordination environments are responsible for the observed effects, and it is therefore not possible to formulate design rules for selecting or synthesizing new candidates.

The choice of building blocks determines the coordination environment and hydrogen-bonding capacity that the resulting framework can present to the perovskite, and the three used here were selected to vary these systematically while retaining a common structural motif. 1,3,5-Triformylphloroglucinol serves as the trialdehyde node in all three frameworks. Its C3-symmetric geometry directs the formation of hexagonally ordered networks, and its three hydroxyl groups, positioned ortho to the aldehyde functions, permit the keto-enol tautomerism that stabilizes β-ketoenamine linkages against hydrolysis, giving frameworks of unusual chemical robustness [37]. Condensation with p-phenylenediamine yields the simplest of the three networks, in which a rigid, minimally functionalized aryl linker provides extended π-conjugation and a high density of nodes but few sites capable of specific interaction with the perovskite precursors. Boc-PDA introduces a bulky carbamate substituent on the same aryl backbone, adding steric volume and carbonyl oxygen atoms that can act as Lewis-basic sites while retaining the aromatic character of the linker [38]. 2,5-Dimethoxyterephthalohydrazide differs more substantially: its two hydrazide groups each provide a carbonyl oxygen and two nitrogen atoms capable of coordination and hydrogen bonding, and the two methoxy substituents are electron-donating and supply further oxygen donors [39]. It therefore presents the richest combination of coordination and hydrogen-bonding motifs of the three, and the highest density of sites available to interact with Pb2+ centers and with the methylammonium and iodide species in the precursor solution. Comparing these three frameworks within one device platform thus separates the contribution of the linker chemistry from that of the common node, which is the basis of the structure–property correlation presented in this work. The molecular structures of the three building blocks are shown in Figure 1.

In this work, we address these gaps by systematically engineering MAPbI3 crystallization through the incorporation of three distinct COFs, each formed by condensation of 1,3,5-triformylphloroglucinol (Tp) with 2,5-dimethoxyterephthalohydrazide (DMTH), Boc-PDA phenylenediamine (Boc-PDA), and 1,3,5-triformylphloroglucinol (Tp). These building blocks give frameworks with different linkage motifs and pore chemistries, spanning hydrazone and β-ketoenamine linkages, and therefore different electronic environments and coordination sites for the perovskite precursor species. DMTH-COF introduces methoxy-substituted hydrazide units that act as electron-donating and coordinating groups, potentially slowing crystal growth and favoring larger grain formation. Boc-PDA-COF offers protected amine functionalities that can be deprotected to expose reactive sites, allowing controlled interaction with the perovskite lattice. Tp-based frameworks typically form highly ordered, hexagonally porous β-ketoenamine COFs, which can serve as rigid templates for perovskite nucleation. By integrating these COFs directly into the MAPbI3 precursor and employing a controlled spin-coating process, we perform a comparative study of how COF chemistry influences crystallization kinetics, grain size, film morphology, defect passivation, optical properties, and device stability. We show that COF-assisted crystallization leads to enlarged grains, reduced grain-boundary density, and suppressed non-radiative recombination, with DMTH-based COFs in particular yielding the most pronounced improvements in film quality and device performance. The resulting mesoscopic n-i-p PSCs exhibit enhanced PCE and markedly improved stability under prolonged illumination and ambient humidity. This work provides strong evidence that rationally designed COFs can serve as powerful crystallization regulators and defect-passivating scaffolds for MAPbI3, providing a structurally tunable platform to simultaneously engineer morphology, electronic structure, and stability in perovskite solar cells. The novelty of this study lies in three key aspects. First, we employ COFs as bulk additives within the MAPbI3 precursor solution rather than as separately deposited interfacial layers. As set out in the preceding discussion, this distinction is consequential: a bulk additive acts during nucleation and growth and is therefore distributed among the grain boundaries throughout the film, whereas a deposited layer acts only at the surface and requires an additional processing step. Second, we present a systematic comparison of three chemically and structurally distinct hydrazone- and β-ketoenamine-linked COFs, prepared from DMTH, Boc-PDA and p-phenylenediamine with 1,3,5-triformylphloroglucinol, within the same MAPbI3 platform, directly correlating framework structure with grain growth statistics, vibrational signatures, optical response, wetting behavior and device-level stability. Third, we show that an optimized COF (DMTH) can simultaneously deliver micrometer-scale grains, reduced microstrain, enhanced hydrophobicity and that the resulting energy-level alignment at the perovskite/HTL interface is consistent with more efficient hole extraction. Together, these advances position COF-based bulk doping as a previously underexplored but highly effective strategy for integrated microstructural and interfacial engineering in perovskite photovoltaics.

Fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO)–coated glass substrates (sheet resistance 7–10 Ω sq−1, Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA)) were patterned by wet chemical etching using HCl and Zn powder. The substrates were then sequentially cleaned in DI water, acetone, and isopropanol (10 min each, ultrasonic bath) and dried in a vacuum oven at 110 °C for 15 min. A compact TiO2 (c-TiO2) precursor solution was prepared by adding titanium isopropoxide (380 μL) dropwise into ethanol (2.56 mL) under continuous stirring. In a separate vial, diluted HCl (340 μL, HCl: water = 3:1 v/v) was mixed with ethanol (2.52 mL). The acidic ethanol solution was then added dropwise to the titanium isopropoxide solution under vigorous stirring, followed by an additional 30 min of stirring to obtain a homogeneous, transparent sol. The TiO2 precursor was spin-coated onto the cleaned FTO substrates at 2000 rpm for 30 s, as shown in Figure 2. The resulting films were dried at 100 °C and then sintered at 450 °C for 40 min to form the c-TiO2 layer. To improve interfacial contact between the compact and mesoporous layers, the c-TiO2-coated substrates were immersed in a 40 mM aqueous TiCl4 solution at 70 °C for 30 min, rinsed, and annealed at 450 °C for 30 min. The mesoporous TiO2 (m-TiO2) scaffold was deposited by spin-coating a diluted TiO2 paste (Dyesol (Queanbeyan, NSW, Australia) 18NR-T) at 4000 rpm. The paste was first dispersed in ethanol (1 g in 5 mL) by repeated sonication and stirring until a uniform suspension was obtained. The m-TiO2-coated substrates were subsequently calcined at 500 °C for 1 h. The patterned FTO substrates gave a device area of 0.50 cm2, defined by the overlap of the FTO and Au electrodes; J–V characterization was performed through a metal aperture mask, as described in Section 2.6.

Three COFs were synthesized via solvothermal condensation. These COFs were specifically selected to provide distinct pore chemistries and coordination environments, enabling a systematic investigation of how COF structure directs MAPbI3 nucleation and grain growth.

DMTH-based COF (DMTH-COF). DMTH (26 mg, 0.102 mmol, 1.43 equiv) and Tp (15 mg, 0.071 mmol, 1.00 equiv) were dissolved in a mixture of mesitylene (4 mL), 1,4-dioxane (2 mL) and acetic acid (0.6 mL) in a glovebox. The mixture was sonicated for 10 min, transferred to a sealed vessel and heated at 140 °C for 72 h (28.3 mg, 77%). The resulting yellow precipitate was collected by centrifugation, washed with ethanol (4 × 10 mL) and acetone (4 × 10 mL), and dried under vacuum at 75 °C for 12 h.

Boc-PDA-based COF (Boc-PDA-COF). Boc-PDA (30 mg, 0.144 mmol, 1.38 equiv), Tp (22 mg, 0.105 mmol, 1.00 equiv) and PTSA (2 mg, 0.012 mmol, 0.11 equiv) were combined in 1,4-dioxane (2 mL) and mesitylene (4 mL) in a glovebox. After sonication and degassing, the mixture was heated at 100 °C for 48 h (26.7 mg, 87%). The precipitate was isolated by centrifugation, washed with ethanol (4 × 10 mL) and acetone (4 × 10 mL), and dried under vacuum at 75 °C for 12 h.

Tp-based COF (Tp-COF). p-Phenylenediamine (16.2 mg, 0.150 mmol, 1.43 equiv) and Tp (22 mg, 0.105 mmol, 1.00 equiv) were dissolved in mesitylene (4 mL), 1,4-dioxane (2 mL) and acetic acid (0.3 mL) in a glovebox. After 10 min of sonication and degassing the mixture was heated at 120 °C for 72 h. The precipitate was collected by centrifugation, washed with ethanol (4 × 10 mL) and acetone (4 × 10 mL), and dried under vacuum at 75 °C for 12 h (25.4 mg, 80%).

The three frameworks were prepared by condensation with 1,3,5-triformylphloroglucinol (Tp). Those formed with DMTH and Boc-PDA are denoted DMTH-COF and Boc-PDA-COF after the hydrazide or amine partner, while the framework formed with p-phenylenediamine is denoted Tp-COF. For brevity, perovskite films and devices containing them are labeled MAPbI3–DMTH, MAPbI3–Boc-PDA and MAPbI3–Tp throughout.

paragraphs.section: 2.4. Preparation of MAPbI3 and COF–MAPbI3 Solutions
paragraphs.text: MAPbI3 precursor solutions were prepared outside the glovebox under ambient conditions at approximately 20% relative humidity. For pristine MAPbI3, MAI (0.19 g, 1.195 mmol, 0.92 equiv) and PbI2 (0.60 g, 1.302 mmol, 1.00 equiv) were dissolved in a mixed solvent of DMF (0.8 mL) and DMSO (0.2 mL), giving nominal concentrations of 1.20 M and 1.30 M, respectively, and stirred at 800 rpm and 60 °C for 2 h to obtain a clear solution. For COF-doped MAPbI3, the COF (0.5 mg, corresponding to 0.5 mg mL−1 or 0.063 wt% of the total solute mass) was dispersed in 1.0 mL of the MAPbI3 precursor solution by sonication for 30 min to yield a homogeneous ink. The dispersion was then stirred at 800 rpm and 60 °C for 2 h and passed through a 0.45 μm PTFE filter prior to deposition.

paragraphs.section: 2.4. Preparation of MAPbI3 and COF–MAPbI3 Solutions
paragraphs.text: Perovskite films were deposited onto the m-TiO2/FTO substrates by a two-step spin-coating protocol. The COF–MAPbI3 ink was first spin-coated at 3000 rpm for 30 s. The spinning speed was then briefly reduced to 500 rpm for 2 s, during which 0.5 mL of chlorobenzene (antisolvent) was quickly dropped onto the rotating substrate. The speed was subsequently increased again to 3000 rpm for 30 s to remove excess solvent and promote rapid crystallization. The resulting films were annealed at 110 °C for 25 min to ensure complete conversion to MAPbI3. Control MAPbI3 films (without COF) were prepared using the same protocol but without COF addition. The final film thickness was ~500 nm, as determined by profilometry. The controlled incorporation of COFs into the MAPbI3 precursor at low loading enables us to probe how COF scaffolding influences nucleation, grain coalescence, and defect formation without significantly altering the bulk composition of the perovskite.

The resulting mesoscopic PSCs with the architecture FTO/c-TiO2/m-TiO2/perovskite/Spiro-OMeTAD/Au were fabricated. The hole-transporting layer (HTL) solution was prepared by dissolving Spiro-OMeTAD (72.4 mg) in chlorobenzene (1 mL), followed by the addition of 4-tert-butylpyridine (TBP, 28.8 μL) and a LiTFSI solution (17.3 μL of 450 mg mL−1 LiTFSI in acetonitrile). This HTL solution was spin-coated onto the COF:MAPbI3 (or pristine MAPbI3) layer at 3500 rpm for 30 s and dried at 60 °C for 15 min. Finally, a 100 nm Au top electrode was thermally evaporated through a shadow mask at a deposition rate of 0.3–0.5 Å s−1 under a base pressure of ~1 × 10−6 Torr. The active area of each device was 0.50 cm2, defined by the overlap of the FTO and Au electrodes.

The crystal structure of the perovskite films was analyzed using a Proto A-XRD diffractometer equipped with a Cu Kα source (λ = 1.5406 Å) and a scintillation counter detector. Instrumental broadening was not subtracted from the measured full widths at half maximum. The crystallite sizes reported in Table 1 therefore represent apparent values and constitute lower bounds on the true coherent domain size. Since all films were measured on the same instrument under identical optical configuration, the relative comparison between samples is unaffected. UV–Vis absorption spectra of perovskite films on FTO were recorded with a Shimadzu UV-2550 spectrophotometer. Surface morphology, elemental composition, and elemental mapping were examined using a Zeiss field-emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM) operated at 20 kV. Film thicknesses were measured with a KLA-Tencor surface profilometer. Steady-state photoluminescence (PL) spectra were collected on a Horiba Fluorolog spectrometer equipped with a 532 W xenon lamp. Raman spectra were recorded using a Renishaw inVia spectrometer (532 nm excitation). Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectra were recorded using a PerkinElmer Spectrum 400 spectrometer equipped with a diamond attenuated total reflectance (ATR) accessory. A background spectrum of the clean, empty ATR crystal was collected before sample measurement and subtracted automatically by the instrument software. No post-acquisition atmospheric compensation for water vapor or CO2 was applied. External quantum efficiency (EQE) measurements were performed using an Enli Technology QE-R system. Current density–voltage characteristics were recorded using a Keithley 2400 source meter under simulated AM1.5G illumination at 100 mW cm−2. Both scan directions were measured in a single continuous sweep cycle over the range −0.24 to 1.19 V at a scan rate of 0.286 V s−1 with no settling delay between the voltage step and the current measurement, and identical conditions were applied to all devices. Measurements were performed through a metal aperture mask defining the active area. The hysteresis index was calculated as HI = (PCE reverse − PCE forward)/PCE reverse.

X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis was employed to elucidate the crystallographic structure, phase purity, and microstructural evolution of MAPbI3 thin films in the presence of different COF additives. Figure 3 compares the diffraction patterns of pristine MAPbI3 with those of MAPbI3 films doped with low concentrations of COFs derived from DMTH, Boc-PDA, and Tp. All samples exhibit a consistent set of well-defined reflections at 2θ ≈ 14.26°, 20.04°, 22.95°, 24.53°, 28.04°, 31.92°, 34.05°, 40.24°, 43.12°, and 50.13°, which can be indexed to the (110), (112), (202), (211), (220), (310), (321), (224), (314), and (404) planes of the tetragonal MAPbI3 phase (ICDD 01-084-2960) [40,41]. The absence of additional peaks, particularly the PbI2 (001) reflection at ~12.7° or any broad amorphous features, confirms that the incorporation of COFs does not generate detectable secondary phases or disrupt the perovskite framework within the resolution of our measurements. This is a critical result: it demonstrates that the COF additives, at the concentrations used here, are structurally compatible with MAPbI3 and can be used to manipulate crystallization without sacrificing phase purity. Beyond phase identification, the XRD patterns provide quantitative insight into how COF chemistry influences the crystallization kinetics, crystalline coherence, and lattice strain of MAPbI3.

The lattice parameters, the crystallite size (D) calculated from the (220) peak, and microstrain (ϵ), of perovskite films were estimated using the following equation reported elsewhere [42,43,44]:(1)D = 0.9λ / (β cos θ)(2)ε = β / (4 tan θ)(3)d = λ / (2 sin θ)(4)1 / d2 = (h2 + k2) / a2 + l2 / c2 where λ is the X-ray wavelength (0.15406 nm), θ is the Bragg angle (in radians; here evaluated near θ ≈ 28.5°), β is the FWHM (in radians) of the chosen diffraction peak, and (hkl) are the Miller indices corresponding to the tetragonal lattice parameters a and c. The quantity D obtained from Equation 1 is the coherent scattering domain size, that is, the length scale over which the lattice diffracts as a single periodic unit and is distinct from the physical grain size determined below by FE-SEM. Values of D are uncorrected for instrumental broadening. D and ε are estimated here under the limiting assumptions of size-only and strain-only broadening, respectively, and are therefore indicative parameters rather than a full deconvolution of the two contributions. The extracted lattice parameters, FWHM values, crystallite sizes, and microstrain for all samples are summarized in Table 1.

The lattice parameters remain essentially invariant across all samples, with (a ≈ 8.895) Å and (c ≈ 12.758) Å, confirming that the introduction of Tp, Boc-PDA, or DMTH does not alter the average tetragonal MAPbI3 crystal structure. By contrast, the FWHM, crystallite size (D), and microstrain ε show a clear and systematic dependence on COF chemistry. Pristine MAPbI3 exhibits a relatively broad FWHM of 0.23°, corresponding to an average crystallite size of 35.6 nm and a microstrain of 3.56 × 10−3. Upon incorporation of Tp-COF, the FWHM decreases to 0.18°, and the crystallite size increases to 45.49 nm, accompanied by a reduction in microstrain to 2.76 × 10−3. Boc-PDA-COF further improves these parameters, yielding (D = 48.17) nm and ε = 2.53 × 10−3 (FWHM = 0.17°). The most pronounced effect is observed for the DMTH-modified film, which displays the narrowest peak (FWHM = 0.15°), the largest crystallite size (54.59 nm), and the lowest microstrain (2.26 × 10−3). The crystallite sizes obtained here, 35.6–54.6 nm, are an order of magnitude smaller than the mean grain sizes of 0.36–1.00 μm determined by FE-SEM in the following section, as expected since each grain accommodates multiple coherently diffracting domains. Both quantities increase in the same order across the additive series, indicating that the COFs enlarge the grains and improve the crystalline coherence within them at the same time.

This systematic evolution, characterized by larger crystallite size (D) and smaller microstrain (ε) from pristine MAPbI3 to Tp-, Boc-PDA-, and finally DMTH-modified films, provides strong quantitative evidence that COF chemistry governs MAPbI3 crystallization kinetics and defect formation. The Tp-based system already acts as an effective scaffold, promoting more coherent crystalline growth and partially relaxing lattice distortion. Introducing Boc-PDA further enriches the framework with amino functionality, enhancing interactions with PbI2/MAI species and leading to a further increase in crystallite size and strain relief. DMTH-COF, which combines methoxy-substituted aromatic rings with hydrazide groups, exerts the strongest effect: its richer coordination and hydrogen-bonding environment most effectively regulates nucleation and supports the growth of larger, more ordered perovskite domains with minimal residual strain. The XRD and extracted microstructural parameters show that all three COFs preserve the tetragonal MAPbI3 phase while progressively sharpening the diffraction peaks, enlarging the crystallites, and reducing microstrain. Among them, DMTH-COF stands out as the most efficient crystallization regulator, delivering the largest coherent domain size and the lowest lattice distortion. This structural optimization, namely phase-pure tetragonal MAPbI3 with enlarged grains and reduced microstrain, provides the crystallographic foundation for the improved photophysical properties and device performance observed in the subsequent PL and photovoltaic measurements [45].

Raman spectroscopy was employed to probe how COF additives affect the molecular and lattice dynamics of MAPbI3, complementing the XRD analysis of long-range order. Spectra were collected using a confocal Raman microscope with a 532 nm laser (200 mW) in the 0–500 cm−1 range, which captures the key inorganic framework vibrations and MA+-related modes while avoiding strong substrate contributions. Figure 4 compares the Raman response of pristine MAPbI3 with that of films prepared with DMTH, Boc-PDA, and Tp-based COFs. In all cases, the spectra exhibit characteristic low-wavenumber bands that are consistent with the tetragonal MAPbI3 phase reported in the literature [46,47]. The Raman spectra are dominated in the low-wavenumber region by distinct features at approximately 36, 54, 83, and 112 cm−1 [48,49,50]. These bands arise mainly from Pb–I stretching and bending vibrations within the corner-sharing [PbI6]4− octahedral framework, together with lattice modes involving coupled displacements of the MA+ cations [48]. The preservation of these sharp, phase-specific vibrational signatures, together with the absence of additional peaks associated with PbI2 or other degradation products, is fully consistent with the XRD results and confirms that all COF-treated films retain the tetragonal MAPbI3 perovskite structure. Although the overall vibrational fingerprint of MAPbI3 is preserved, careful inspection reveals systematic COF-induced modifications in both peak position and line shape.

In particular, the Pb–I lattice modes shift progressively toward lower wavenumbers in the COF-treated films. To quantify this, each band was fitted with a Lorentzian profile over an identical spectral window for all four samples, and the extracted positions are given in Table 2.

Lorentzian fitting was performed to quantify the positions of the selected low-wavenumber Raman bands (Table 2). The lower-frequency mode was located at 58.22 cm−1 for pristine MAPbI3 and shifted to 55.97, 55.44, and 54.71 cm−1 after modification with Tp, Boc-PDA, and DMTH, respectively. The corresponding red shifts were 2.25, 2.78, and 3.51 cm−1. Similarly, the higher-frequency mode shifted from 121.88 cm−1 for the pristine film to 119.93, 118.17, and 115.88 cm−1 for the Tp-, Boc-PDA-, and DMTH-modified films, respectively. These shifts are consistent with modification of the local Pb–I vibrational environment and may reflect changes in lattice strain, bonding interactions, or the electrostatic environment surrounding the PbI6 octahedra [47]. Their magnitudes follow the same ordering as the crystallite size and microstrain from XRD and the grain size from FE-SEM, providing independent vibrational evidence for the progressive relaxation of the Pb–I framework.

The relative changes among the three COFs are particularly revealing. The 36 and 83 cm−1 features were not analyzed quantitatively; the former, because it does not follow a consistent trend across the series and the latter because its low intensity and overlap with the 112 cm−1 mode preclude a reliable fit. The Tp-modified film already exhibits a modest narrowing and slight intensity enhancement of the lattice modes compared to the pristine reference, suggesting that even a relatively rigid, less functionalized COF can improve vibrational coherence. The Boc-PDA-COF system further sharpens the Pb–I features and strengthens the modes associated with MA+ libration, which is consistent with amino-containing linkers interacting more directly with the organic cations [51]. The DMTH-containing films show the most pronounced effects, with the largest narrowing and the strongest intensity increase in the mixed Pb–I–MA region. This behavior can be attributed to the richer hydrogen-bonding and coordination landscape provided by the methoxy and hydrazide groups in DMTH-COF, which are well suited to interact simultaneously with the inorganic framework and the MA+ cations [52]. These interactions likely damp large-amplitude MA+ reorientations and reduce dynamic disorder at grain boundaries, leading to a more coherent vibrational response.

The Raman data provide molecular-level support for the proposed COF-assisted crystallization mechanism. The preservation of phase-specific modes indicates that the perovskite lattice is not disrupted by COF incorporation. The red shifts and peak sharpening demonstrate that COFs relieve local strain and suppress vibrational disorder, in agreement with the larger crystallite sizes and lower microstrain extracted from XRD. Among the three systems, DMTH-COF stands out as the most effective modifier of the vibrational landscape, which aligns with its superior impact on grain growth and defect suppression. These spectroscopic signatures strongly suggest that COFs act as static structural templates during film formation and also as dynamic modulators of lattice and cation motions. This dual role is highly relevant for device performance, since reduced vibrational disorder and stabilized MA+ dynamics are expected to lower non-radiative recombination, hinder ion migration, and ultimately contribute to the enhanced photostability and efficiency observed in the corresponding solar cells [53].

To elucidate how COF incorporation modifies the microstructure of MAPbI3, we examined the surface morphology of the perovskite films by field-emission scanning electron microscopy, as shown in Figure 5. All samples were prepared by spin-coating on TiO2-based substrates under identical conditions, with low loadings of COFs chosen to promote crystallization while preserving the underlying perovskite lattice. The COFs studied here, DMTH, Boc-PDA, and Tp, are relatively under-explored in the context of perovskite thin films, which allows us to directly assess their potential as morphology-directing additives. The pristine MAPbI3 film (Figure 5a) exhibits a compact but fine-grained morphology, with grains averaging around 360 nm. Although the surface coverage is reasonably uniform, the high density of grain boundaries and the presence of small voids and irregular grain shapes are evident. Such features are typically associated with elevated densities of grain-boundary defects, which can act as non-radiative recombination centers and scattering sites, limiting carrier mobility and diffusion length in photovoltaic devices [54].

Upon incorporation of COF additives, the morphology changes dramatically. The Tp-doped film (Figure 5b) shows grains that have grown to roughly 670 nm on average, with improved grain coalescence and fewer visible intergranular gaps. Boc-PDA-COF further accentuates this trend (Figure 5c), producing grains of about 910 nm, as well as a noticeably smoother and more continuous surface. The most pronounced effect is observed for DMTH-COF (Figure 5d), where the average grain size reaches about 1 µm, corresponding to more than a threefold increase compared to the pristine film. In this case, the surface is dominated by large, faceted grains with well-defined boundaries, and the film appears nearly pinhole-free at the micron scale. These systematic morphological changes indicate that the COFs strongly influence the nucleation and growth kinetics of MAPbI3. The enlarged grains and reduced boundary density suggest that COFs act as crystallization regulators or soft templates during film formation [55]. Mechanistically, this behavior can be rationalized by the functional groups and porous architectures intrinsic to these COFs. The hydrazide and imine (C=N) functionalities provide coordination sites for Pb2+ species, while amino and methoxy groups can form hydrogen bonds with MA+ cations or halide anions [56,57]. Such interactions are expected to moderate the rate of nucleation, promote the growth of fewer but larger nuclei, and stabilize the evolving grain boundaries [58]. At the same time, the porous and π-conjugated networks of the COFs likely facilitate more uniform solvent evaporation and enhance mass transport during the crystallization step, which further supports the formation of large, well-connected grains [59].

Incorporation of COFs therefore affects the geometric microstructure and the defect landscape. Fewer grain boundaries and smoother interfaces imply a lower density of undercoordinated Pb2+ and halide vacancies at the surface and interfaces [60]. The coordination bonding between COF C=N groups and Pb2+ ions, coupled with hydrogen bonding between COF −NH2 groups and halides, can effectively passivate both shallow and deep traps at and near grain boundaries [61]. This structural passivation is consistent with the observed narrowing of XRD peaks and reduced microstrain. From a device standpoint, the grain enlargement and improved surface quality induced by COF additives are expected to have several beneficial consequences. Larger grains and fewer boundaries reduce non-radiative recombination pathways, allowing photogenerated carriers to travel longer distances before recombination, which should enhance charge collection and increase open-circuit voltage [62]. Better grain connectivity and reduced porosity facilitate more efficient charge transport across the perovskite layer, which can translate into higher fill factors and improved device performance [63]. Additionally, the partial hydrophobic character introduced by certain COF moieties, particularly in the DMTH-modified films, may help to improve environmental stability by limiting moisture ingress along grain boundaries [64]. Importantly, the use of DMTH, Boc-PDA, and Tp as direct dopants inside the perovskite layer represents a distinct approach compared with most previous studies, which have concentrated on more conventional imine-linked COFs used mainly at interfaces or as surface passivation layers [65,66]. Here, the COFs actively guide bulk film formation and microstructure rather than only decorating the surface. The FE-SEM results thus provide direct visual evidence that COF chemistry can be harnessed to engineer the grain-scale architecture of MAPbI3, laying a structural foundation for the improved optoelectronic properties and photovoltaic performance that will be discussed in the following sections.

Figure 6 shows the grain size distributions of COF-modified MAPbI3 films and quantitatively confirms the strong grain-growth effect inferred from the FE-SEM images. The histograms were obtained by measuring individual grains from plan-view FE-SEM micrographs and plotting the frequency of occurrence as a function of equivalent grain diameter for MAPbI3 films doped with (a) Boc-PDA-COF and (b) DMTH-COF. In both cases, the distributions exhibit the characteristic positive skew typical of solution-processed perovskites and are well described by lognormal fits, indicating that nucleation and growth follow a multiplicative process. The Boc-PDA-COF film displays a mean grain size of approximately 0.91 μm, with the majority of grains clustered around 0.6–0.8 μm and relatively few sub-500 nm crystallites, indicating efficient suppression of excessive nucleation and enhanced grain coalescence. The DMTH-COF film shows an even more pronounced shift toward larger grains, with a mean diameter near 1.0 μm and a distribution that is both broadened toward larger sizes and depleted of small grains. This evolution of the lognormal parameters between Boc-PDA-COF and DMTH-COF provides strong evidence that COF chemistry systematically modulates the statistics of MAPbI3 grain growth: DMTH-COF, with its more strongly coordinating hydrazide and methoxy functionalities, promotes fewer nucleation events and more extensive lateral growth per nucleus, yielding a microstructure dominated by large, well-connected grains and a significantly reduced grain-boundary density.

To evaluate the elemental composition and spatial distribution within the DMTH-COF-modified MAPbI3 film, we conducted energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX). The summed spectrum (Figure 7b) is dominated by characteristic iodine and lead emissions, yielding atomic fractions of 74.31% I and 24.25% Pb. The resulting Pb:I ratio of 1:3.06 aligns closely with the nominal 1:3 stoichiometry of MAPbI3, confirming that the COF additive does not disrupt the bulk inorganic framework [67]. This compositional stability is critical: deviations from ideal stoichiometry typically generate halide vacancies or metallic lead clusters, both of which act as deep trap states and exacerbate non-radiative recombination. Consequently, the enhanced carrier lifetime and device performance cannot be attributed to compositional shifts in the bulk perovskite, but rather to the structural and interfacial improvements identified via our diffraction and morphological analyses. The elemental maps further demonstrate that this near-ideal stoichiometry is uniform across the film’s microstructure. Both iodine and lead signals (Figure 7c,d) are distributed continuously across the grain interiors and boundaries. We observe no regions of halide depletion or lead enrichment, which would indicate halide segregation or PbI2 accumulation at the grain edges.

The absence of such segregation is consistent with the XRD data, where no residual PbI2 reflection was detected at 12.7°, confirming that the enlarged grains induced by the COF remain compositionally homogeneous. Signals for nitrogen (1.11 at.%) and oxygen (0.33 at.%) were also detected, and their corresponding maps (Figure 7e,f) show a uniform distribution across the imaged area. Because light elements are notoriously difficult to quantify accurately by EDX due to severe self-absorption and low detector efficiency at the low energies of the N Kα (0.392 keV) and O Kα (0.525 keV) lines, these absolute values should be treated as qualitative. However, the spatial mapping is highly informative: the lack of localized N or O accumulation confirms that the additive does not aggregate into discrete, phase-separated organic domains. Instead, the COF remains homogeneously dispersed throughout the film. Together, these results indicate that the additive facilitates uniform crystallization and surface passivation without perturbing the phase purity or bulk composition of the perovskite absorber.

Water contact angle measurements were performed to quantitatively examine how COF doping modifies the surface wettability and, by implication, the surface energy and moisture affinity of MAPbI3 thin films. Because MAPbI3 degradation is strongly accelerated by humidity and frequently initiates at exposed surfaces and grain boundaries [68], even relatively small changes in surface hydrophilicity or hydrophobicity can have a disproportionate impact on long-term stability and interfacial reliability in devices [69]. In this work, three COF-type organic additives based on DMTH, Boc-PDA, and Tp were incorporated into MAPbI3, and their influence on WCA was systematically compared with that of undoped MAPbI3. The WCA analysis therefore provides a direct, macroscopic probe of how COFs alter the outermost surface chemistry and morphology, linking microstructural changes observed by FE-SEM and XRD to the improvements in device performance and stability.

All WCA measurements were carried out using the sessile-drop method on a contact angle goniometer. MAPbI3 and MAPbI3–COF films (MAPbI3–Tp, MAPbI3–Boc-PDA, and MAPbI3–DMTH) were deposited on identically cleaned TiO2/FTO substrates, employing the same precursor concentration, spin parameters, antisolvent timing, and annealing protocol described in the experimental section. A microsyringe was used to gently place small droplets (4 µL) of deionized water onto the film surface without mechanically disturbing the perovskite layer. Representative droplet profiles are shown in Figure 8. The pristine MAPbI3 film (Figure 8a) exhibits a moderate an average contact angle of 65.3°, corresponding to partial wetting and a surface that is neither strongly hydrophilic nor strongly hydrophobic. This behavior is consistent with the mixed ionic and organic nature of MAPbI3 and the presence of polar methylammonium cations and undercoordinated ions at the surface [70]. While such an intermediate WCA favors wetting by typical solution-processed transport layers, it also leaves the surface vulnerable to water adsorption from ambient air, which can initiate hydrolysis and decomposition [71]. This pristine WCA therefore serves as a meaningful baseline for assessing the effect of COF incorporation.

When Tp-based COF is introduced (Figure 8b, MAPbI3–Tp), the water droplet becomes slightly more spherical, and the contact angle increases to about 71.1°. This change reflects a modification of the surface free energy, likely due to the presence of aromatic rings and keto/enolic groups in the Tp-derived network that partially shield polar sites at the perovskite surface or at grain boundaries [72]. Even this modest increase suggests that the COF is not confined to the film interior but influences the near-surface region, either through surface segregation or preferential decoration of grain boundaries that intersect the surface. A more pronounced effect is seen for the film doped with Boc-PDA-derived COF (Figure 8c, MAPbI3–Boc-PDA), where the WCA rises to approximately 78.7°. The Boc-PDA-COF motif introduces bulky aromatic and urethane-like groups that can reorient at the film–air interface and alter local packing [73]. The higher WCA indicates a more hydrophobic surface, which reduces direct contact between water molecules and polar perovskite sites. Combined with FE-SEM evidence of smoother, denser morphologies and XRD indications of improved crystallinity, this increase in WCA supports the interpretation that Boc-PDA-based COF effectively passivates surface defects and grain boundaries, thereby limiting moisture access to reactive sites and contributing to enhanced stability.

The most dramatic change in wettability is observed for the DMTH-containing film (Figure 8d, MAPbI3–DMTH), where the WCA reaches approximately 96°. The significantly more spherical droplet profile reveals a highly hydrophobic surface compared to the pristine and other COF-modified films. Given the functional architecture of DMTH-COF, which combines methoxy and hydrazide groups within a conjugated framework, this strong hydrophobic response can be attributed to a combination of topographical smoothing, partial coverage of hydrophilic perovskite sites by the COF, and reorientation of less polar COF moieties toward the outer surface [74]. The concomitant microstructural improvements seen in FE-SEM for DMTH-doped films, including large, well-coalesced grains with minimal pinholes, further reinforce the view that DMTH-COF not only regulates bulk crystallization but also significantly reorganizes the surface region. The series of WCA images and corresponding values reveal a clear, monotonic tuning of surface wettability with COF chemistry. Relative to pristine MAPbI3, all three COF-doped films exhibit higher contact angles, confirming that COF addition is an effective strategy for increasing the hydrophobic character of the perovskite surface. This trend is particularly pronounced for DMTH-COF, which yields a hydrophobic surface regime. When these results are considered alongside FE-SEM (denser, larger grains), XRD (enlarged crystallites and reduced microstrain), PL (enhanced radiative recombination and reduced non-radiative loss), and device performance data (higher Jsc, FF, PCE, together with improved operational stability), a coherent picture emerges. COF additives simultaneously refine the bulk microstructure and engineer the outermost surface to be less accessible to moisture and other environmental stressors [75]. The WCA measurements therefore provide an essential mechanistic link between molecular-scale surface modification by COFs and the macroscopic gains in efficiency and durability observed in MAPbI3 perovskite solar cells.

UV–Vis spectrophotometry was employed to elucidate how COF additives influence the optical response and band structure of MAPbI3 thin films. Absorbance spectra were recorded using a double-beam spectrophotometer over 400–900 nm with a 1 nm resolution. All films examined by UV–Vis spectroscopy were prepared using the same perovskite precursor concentration and an identical additive concentration of 0.5 mg mL−1, under the same deposition and annealing conditions, allowing direct comparison of their measured spectra. The four spectra coincide below the absorption edge and separate only above it, confirming that the differences in absorbance arise from the optical response of the films rather than from any difference in thickness or absorber loading. As shown in Figure 9, all spin-coated films exhibit strong absorption across the visible spectrum with a pronounced onset near 750–780 nm, consistent with the direct bandgap transition of MAPbI3 arising from electronic transitions between valence-band states derived primarily from I 5p and Pb 6s orbitals and conduction-band states dominated by Pb 6p orbitals [76,77]. The high absorbance in this region reflects the intrinsically large absorption coefficient of hybrid lead halide perovskites [78]. The pristine MAPbI3 film presents a relatively sharp absorption edge and smooth spectral profile. Upon incorporation of Tp, Boc-PDA, and DMTH-based COFs, the overall absorbance in the visible range increases while the absorption edge remains unchanged. Among the modified samples, the DMTH-containing film displays the highest absorbance over a broad wavelength range. This enhancement can be attributed to improved film coverage and crystallinity, as corroborated by FE-SEM and XRD, and to additional electronic interactions between the π-conjugated COF and the perovskite lattice that increase the effective oscillator strength and reduce scattering losses [79].

To quantify the impact on the optical bandgap, the absorption data were analyzed using Tauc plots for direct-bandgap semiconductors, according to(5)(αhν)n = A(hν − Eg) where α = Absorption coefficient, h = Planck’s constant, ν = Frequency, n = Exponent related to the transition type, A = Constant, and Eg = Band gap energy. Extrapolation of the linear region of ((αhν)2) versus (hν) gives bandgap values of 1.567 eV for pristine MAPbI3, 1.567 eV for the Tp-doped film, 1.567 eV for the Boc-PDA-doped film and 1.560 eV for the DMTH-doped film, equal to within 7 meV (inset of Figure 9). The absorption onset is therefore unaffected by COF incorporation, as expected for additives too large to be accommodated on a lattice site, and consistent with the invariant tetragonal lattice parameters reported in Table 1.

These optical trends are significant for several reasons. First, the preservation of a sharp absorption onset and the absence of additional sub-bandgap features confirm that COF incorporation does not generate optically active defect phases, which is consistent with the phase-pure XRD patterns and clean vibrational signatures seen in the Raman data. Second, the increased absorbance across the visible range reflects improved film coverage and crystallinity, which enhances photon harvesting within the same spectral window and contributes to the higher short-circuit current density [80]. Third, the strongest effects are observed for the DMTH-modified film, which is consistent with its superior structural and vibrational characteristics. The methoxy and hydrazide functionalities in DMTH-COF are expected to donate electron density and form hydrogen bonds at the perovskite surface, stabilizing the lattice and slightly perturbing the band edges. The combination of higher absorbance, an unchanged bandgap and maintained spectral cleanliness reflects a favorable modification of the perovskite morphology without alteration of its electronic structure. These optical improvements, when considered together with the enlarged grain sizes, reduced microstrain, and more coherent lattice dynamics, point to a coherent picture in which COF-engineered MAPbI3 films are better suited to high-efficiency and potentially more stable perovskite solar cells, with improved visible-light absorption.

Photoluminescence spectroscopy provides a direct probe of radiative and non-radiative recombination processes in perovskite absorbers and is therefore a sensitive indicator of defect density, trap passivation, and carrier dynamics. Here, steady-state PL measurements were performed on MAPbI3 films spin-coated onto compact/mesoporous TiO2 substrates, with emission collected between 550 and 1000 nm under 532 nm excitation. Figure 10 compares the PL response of pristine MAPbI3 with that of films incorporating DMTH, Boc-PDA, and Tp-based COFs. All three films were prepared at the same additive loading and film thickness and measured under identical excitation conditions, so the absorbed photon flux is comparable across the series. All samples display a dominant emission peak in the 750–800 nm region, consistent with band-edge recombination in tetragonal MAPbI3 [81]. All spectra exhibit a single, intense emission band centered around 772 nm (approximately 1.6 eV), in excellent agreement with the optical bandgap extracted from UV–Vis measurements.

The nearly invariant PL peak position therefore indicates that Tp, Boc-PDA, and DMTH do not substantially alter the fundamental bandgap of MAPbI3. Accordingly, the differences in the apparent Tauc bandgaps are interpreted as variations in the near-edge optical response rather than evidence of pronounced bandgap narrowing. The observed changes in PL intensity are more reasonably associated with changes in defect-mediated non-radiative recombination and film quality [82]. Furthermore, the absence of secondary peaks or shoulders and the nearly Gaussian line shape indicate minimal contributions from phase impurities, self-trapped excitons, or strong photon reabsorption [83]. This clean, unimodal profile is fully consistent with the phase-pure tetragonal MAPbI3 structure established by XRD and the well-defined vibrational fingerprints observed in Raman spectra. The most striking feature in Figure 10 is the systematic enhancement of PL intensity upon COF incorporation. Relative to pristine MAPbI3, all COF-treated films show significantly higher PL, with the strongest emission observed for the DMTH-modified film, followed by Boc-PDA-COF and then Tp-COF. Since the emission peak position remains essentially unchanged, this increase in PL intensity can be attributed primarily to a reduction in non-radiative recombination pathways [84]. The COF additives improve the internal radiative efficiency of the perovskite by passivating electronic defects that would otherwise act as non-radiative recombination centers. These spectroscopic indications align closely with the structural and morphological trends identified in the previous sections. Structural analysis revealed that COF-treated films possess larger crystallite sizes and lower microstrain than pristine MAPbI3, particularly in the DMTH-COF case. FE-SEM images showed more compact, well-coalesced grains with fewer pinholes for COF-modified films. Such structural improvements are expected to decrease the density of undercoordinated Pb2+ and halide vacancies at grain boundaries, which are known to act as deep traps [85]. The enhanced PL intensity is therefore consistent with a scenario in which COFs, and especially the hydrazide and methoxy functionalities in DMTH-COF, coordinate to undercoordinated Pb2+ sites and participate in hydrogen bonding with MA+ cations, thereby passivating traps and suppressing non-radiative losses [86].

From a device perspective, these PL results are highly relevant. High steady-state PL under open-circuit-like conditions is characteristic of high-quality perovskite absorbers with low non-radiative recombination, which typically correlates with higher open-circuit voltage and improved power conversion efficiency. In operational devices, efficient charge extraction at short circuit leads to PL quenching; thus, the combination of strong PL in stand-alone films and strong quenching in complete devices is a hallmark of optimal absorber/transport-layer coupling [87]. The pronounced PL enhancement in the DMTH-containing films therefore foreshadows the superior photovoltaic performance and stability observed for these devices.

Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy was used to probe chemical interactions between the COFs (DMTH, Boc-PDA, and Tp-based frameworks) and the MAPbI3 lattice at the molecular level. Because the organic sublattice of MAPbI3 plays a central role in hydrogen bonding, ion migration, and structural stability [88], even subtle changes in the vibrational signatures of CH3NH3+ and COF functional groups can reveal how these additives reorganize the local bonding environment and help stabilize the perovskite. Figure 11 shows the FTIR spectra of pristine and COF-modified MAPbI3 films over the mid-IR range. The reference MAPbI3 film displays the expected vibrational fingerprint. The methylammonium (CH3–NH3+) rocking mode appears near 851 cm−1 [89], while prominent C–N stretching modes are observed at approximately 1021 and 1135 cm−1 [90]. A further band arising from the methylammonium cation is detected around 1215 cm−1, and a well-defined N–H bending mode of the ammonium group is located near 1512 cm−1 [46]. At higher wavenumbers, weak features are observed near 1857 and 2091 cm−1. Because the CH3NH3PbI3 lattice contains neither carbonyl nor nitrile functional groups, these features are not assigned to intrinsic C=O or C≡N stretching vibrations of the perovskite [91]. They appear at the same positions and with comparable intensity in all four spectra, including the pristine reference, and lie within the region in which the underlying glass substrate absorbs through Si–O overtone and combination modes [92]. They are therefore attributed to a residual contribution from the underlying glass substrate and are excluded from the structural interpretation of the films. The band near 2372 cm−1 is attributed to the asymmetric stretching vibration of atmospheric CO2 [93]. Its presence is consistent with the fact that no post-acquisition atmospheric correction was applied to the ATR-FTIR spectra.

A broad asymmetric N–H stretching envelope centered around 3190 cm−1 reflects the hydrogen-bonding environment of MA+ within the Pb–I framework [94]. Upon incorporation of COFs, these bands do not disappear or split into new impurity-related features, which indicates that the fundamental perovskite lattice is preserved. Instead, the spectra exhibit systematic shifts in peak positions and changes in relative intensity that can be directly linked to COF–perovskite interactions. All three COF-modified films show noticeable variations in the CH3–NH3+-related modes (rocking, bending, and C–H stretching) and in the C–O and C=O bands. For example, the N–H bending band near 1512 cm−1 slightly shifted and sharpened in the presence of COFs. These shifts are consistent with a change in the hydrogen-bonding strength between MA+ and surrounding iodide ions, as well as with additional hydrogen bonds and weak coordination involving COF functional groups such as hydrazides, Boc-protected amines, and aromatic carbonyls [95].

In the DMTH-modified film, for instance, the C–O and C=O bands show small but reproducible shifts and intensity changes, consistent with partial coordination of the hydrazide and methoxy groups to undercoordinated Pb2+ centers and with altered hydrogen-bonding networks involving MA+ and halides [96]. Similar, though less pronounced, trends are observed for Boc-PDA- and Tp-based films, indicating that all three COFs participate in interfacial interactions but with different strengths and geometries. The broad N–H stretching region around 3190 cm−1 is particularly informative. In pristine MAPbI3, the breadth of this band reflects a distribution of hydrogen-bond strengths between MA+ and iodide (N+–H···I) [97]. Any narrowing or shift in this band upon COF doping points to a more uniform and possibly stronger hydrogen-bonding environment, which is expected to suppress dynamic disorder of the organic cation and reduce the formation of defect-related local environments. The attenuation or modification of certain NH3+ stretching components in COF-containing samples can be interpreted as a consequence of additional N–H···O or N–H···N interactions introduced by the COFs, which partially redistribute the hydrogen-bonding network away from purely MA+–I− contacts [95].

These molecular-level signatures are fully consistent with the broader structural and optoelectronic trends observed in this study. COF incorporation produces larger grains with lower microstrain and smoother, denser films, along with stronger band-edge emission, reduced non-radiative recombination, an unchanged bandgap and enhanced optical absorption. The FTIR evidence of modified CH3NH3+ and C–O/C=O vibrational environments provides the chemical basis for these observations: COFs interact with the perovskite at the grain boundaries and surfaces, coordinating to undercoordinated Pb2+ and participating in hydrogen bonding with MA+ and halides [98]. In doing so, they passivate traps, stabilize the organic–inorganic interface, and suppress vibrational and structural disorder, without disrupting the core PbI6 framework.

X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was used to verify the presence of the DMTH-COF additive after thermal annealing and to evaluate its chemical interaction with the perovskite lattice. Figure 12 displays the high-resolution core-level spectra for both pristine and modified films. The pristine sample shows the I 3d doublet at 619.5 eV (I 3d5/2) and 630.8 eV (I 3d3/2). Incorporation of COF shifts these peaks to 619.8 eV and 631.4 eV, respectively, while the spin–orbit splitting remains approximately 11.6 eV [99]. The Pb 4f spectra exhibit a parallel shift: pristine peaks at 139.1 eV and 143.9 eV move to 139.2 eV and 144.1 eV in the modified film. The spin–orbit splitting stays at ~4.9 eV, and the absence of a signal near 136.8 eV confirms the strict preservation of the Pb2+ state [100]. The uniform shift in both Pb and I core levels, without changes to their splitting, indicates a surface Fermi level shift driven by the electron-donating COF rather than altered Pb–I covalency. The bulk halide sublattice therefore remains intact.

The N 1s spectra confirm the additive’s retention. The pristine film exhibits a single peak at 402.3 eV from the protonated methylammonium (MA+) cation [101]. After modification, the (MA+) peak is shifted to 401.9 eV and a clear second component appears at 399.7 eV. This new feature, 2.2 eV below the ammonium peak, is consistent with a less positively charged nitrogen environment and is therefore assigned to the hydrazide/hydrazone nitrogens in the DMTH framework [102]. Its presence confirms that the organic framework survives the 110 °C anneal. To decouple local chemical effects from uniform surface charging, the internal energy separation between the N 1s and I 3d5/2 core levels was evaluated. This gap increases by 0.7 eV, from 217.2 eV (pristine) to 217.9 eV (modified). This relative shift, combined with the displacement of the MA+ peak, shows that the additive chemically interacts with the perovskite rather than forming a segregated organic phase. The C 1s spectra show only a minor shift from 286.5 eV to 286.6 eV, as expected given the overlap between the dominant MA+ signal and the low-concentration COF (0.063 wt%). The XPS data establish that the DMTH-COF remains within the film, chemically couples to the perovskite at the surfaces or grain boundaries, and leaves the bulk Pb–I structural framework unperturbed. This surface-localized interaction supports the proposed passivation mechanism, explaining the suppressed non-radiative recombination without compromising the bulk lattice integrity.

The energy level diagram in Figure 13 illustrates the charge-extraction pathways in the perovskite solar cell, with a particular focus on the offsets along the hole-transport route. The energy levels shown in Figure 13 are based on literature values and electrochemical estimates rather than direct UPS/KPFM measurements, and are used to illustrate a plausible band-alignment scenario rather than to provide exact work-function values [103]. In the reference stack, the MAPbI3 conduction band minimum (CBM, ≈−3.93 eV) aligns reasonably well with the TiO2 CBM (≈−4.2 eV), which supports efficient electron extraction toward the FTO contact [104]. On the hole side, the MAPbI3 valence band maximum (VBM, ≈−5.43 eV) is offset from the Spiro-OMeTAD HOMO (≈−5.2 eV) and the Au work function (≈−5.1 eV) [105]. This offset of 0.23 eV between the perovskite VBM and the Spiro-OMeTAD HOMO is favorably oriented for hole extraction while remaining small enough to limit the associated energy loss.

DMTH-COF is incorporated within the MAPbI3 absorber rather than as a discrete layer and therefore does not contribute frontier levels to the charge-extraction pathway. The polar hydrazide and methoxy groups in DMTH-COF facilitate the formation of an oriented interfacial dipole at the perovskite surface, locally shifting the vacuum level and tuning the perovskite work function without significantly perturbing the bulk bandgap. This reduces the energy offset between the perovskite VBM and the Spiro-OMeTAD HOMO, which in turn lowers interfacial energy losses, enables a larger fraction of the photovoltage to be harvested, and supports a higher quasi-Fermi level splitting under illumination [106]. The alignment shown in Figure 13 is consistent with the experimental device trends. DMTH-containing cells exhibit higher Voc and fill factor than pristine devices, despite comparable optical bandgaps, indicating that fewer photogenerated carriers are lost to interfacial non-radiative recombination and that the built-in potential is more efficiently utilized. The microstructural advantages of DMTH-COF, comprising micrometer-scale grains, reduced microstrain and enhanced hydrophobicity, reduce the density of recombination-active sites within the absorber, so that a larger fraction of photogenerated holes reaches the Spiro-OMeTAD interface and is subsequently collected at the Au electrode. In parallel, electrons follow a separate, well-aligned route via TiO2 and FTO [107].

The photovoltaic performance of the devices provides an integrated assessment of how COF doping affects the structure, optoelectronic properties, and charge-transport characteristics of MAPbI3. PSCs were fabricated in a standard n–i–p configuration, glass/FTO/c–TiO2/m -TiO2/MAPbI3:COF/Spiro- OMeTAD/Au, using MAPbI3 absorbers prepared without and with COFs (Tp, Boc-PDA-phenylenediamine, and DMTH). All devices were measured under AM 1.5G illumination (100 mW cm−2). From Figure 14 and Table 3, the reference (undoped) MAPbI3 device exhibits a Voc of 1.142 V, a Jsc of 17.53 mA cm−2, a fill factor (FF) of 73.45%, and a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 14.7%. These values are characteristic of solution-processed MAPbI3 cells limited by defect-mediated non-radiative recombination, incomplete light harvesting, and non-ideal series and shunt resistances [108]. Introduction of COF additives leads to a systematic improvement in all figures of merit. The Tp-modified device reaches 15.88% PCE, Boc-PDA-COF-modified devices reach 18.88%, and the DMTH-based device achieves the highest performance with Voc = 1.183 V, Jsc = 22.98 mA cm−2, FF = 76.46%, and PCE = 20.78%. This progression demonstrates that the extent of performance enhancement closely follows the effectiveness of each COF in controlling crystallization, passivating defects, and optimizing interfacial energetics.

The Voc enhancement from 1.142 V to 1.183 V reflects a reduction in non-radiative recombination losses in the bulk and at the interfaces. This is consistent with the strong PL intensity increase observed for COF-treated films, particularly for DMTH-COF, which indicates reduced trap-assisted recombination and higher quasi-Fermi level splitting. The Jsc increase, from 17.53 to 22.98 mA cm−2, arises from a combination of broader and more intense optical absorption and improved carrier collection [80]. UV–Vis spectra showed enhanced absorbance at an unchanged absorption onset for COF-doped films, while XRD and FE-SEM revealed enlarged grain sizes and fewer grain boundaries, both of which promote longer diffusion lengths and lower recombination probabilities. The largest Jsc in DMTH-based devices is therefore a direct manifestation of the most favorable combination of microstructure, defect passivation, and optical response. The fill factor also improves with COF doping, rising from 73.45% in the pristine device to 76.46% in the DMTH-COF case. This improvement is tightly linked to the evolution of series resistance (Rs) and shunt resistance (Rsh). The fill factor also improves with COF doping, rising from 73.45% in the pristine device to 76.46% in the DMTH-COF case. The series resistance extracted from the slope of the reverse-scan J–V curve at Voc falls from 5.5 Ω cm2 in the pristine device to 4.0 Ω cm2 in the DMTH-COF device, a reduction of 27%. The intermediate values obtained for the Tp-COF and Boc-PDA-COF devices, 4.8 and 5.1 Ω cm2, are close to the uncertainty of the extraction, so the comparison is made here between the pristine and DMTH-COF cases.

In parallel, Rsh increases from 5.92 to 7.74 kΩ cm2 with COF doping. Low Rsh in the pristine devices indicates the presence of leakage paths, such as micro-shorts, surface defects, and ion-migration-related shunts [108]. The higher Rsh in COF-modified devices shows that these parasitic channels are significantly suppressed. Morphologically, this corresponds to denser, more uniform films with reduced pinhole density, as seen by FE-SEM, and structurally to fewer extended defects and dislocations, as suggested by the narrowed XRD peaks and reduced microstrain. The concurrent decrease in Rs and increase in Rsh demonstrates that COF additives simultaneously enhance charge-transport pathways and block undesirable leakage routes, which together raise the FF and overall PCE.

The relative performance of the three COFs aligns with their structural and electronic characteristics. Tp-based COFs form ordered, β-ketoenamine networks with hexagonal pores that provide a basic scaffold for more uniform crystal growth and moderate passivation. Boc-PDA-derived COFs introduce aromatic and Boc-protected amine functionalities that more effectively interact with MA+ and Pb2+, leading to larger grains, lower trap density, and better surface passivation, and consequently a substantial jump in PCE to 18.88%. DMTH, containing methoxy-substituted hydrazide groups, goes further by combining strong coordination capability with electron-donating character and good solubility. This enables the formation of flexible, two-dimensional COF networks that intimately coat grain surfaces and interfaces, finely tuning crystallization.

The photovoltaic parameters obtained from forward and reverse J–V sweeps, together with the calculated hysteresis indices, are summarized in Figure 15 and Table 4. The pristine MAPbI3 device shows pronounced scan dependence: its PCE falls from 14.84% in the reverse direction to 11.92% in the forward direction, giving a hysteresis index of 0.197. In MAPbI3 devices, such discrepancies generally arise from a combination of charge trapping, carrier accumulation at the contacts, and redistribution of mobile ionic species during the sweep [85]. Defects including undercoordinated Pb2+ sites and halide vacancies can promote all three processes by introducing trap states and distorting the local electric field.

All three additives reduce the scan dependence, though to different degrees. The hysteresis index drops to 0.161 with Tp, 0.107 with Boc-PDA, and 0.110 with DMTH. The improvement with Tp is modest, whereas Boc-PDA and DMTH nearly halve the hysteresis relative to the control. This suggests that both additives alter the defect and interfacial environment of the perovskite layer in ways that make charge extraction far less sensitive to sweep direction. The raw hysteresis index alone, however, does not tell the full story. Although Boc-PDA gives the marginally lower index, the DMTH device delivers the best absolute performance in both sweep directions, with PCEs of 20.38% and 18.13% under reverse and forward scans, respectively. Weighing hysteresis suppression against absolute efficiency, DMTH therefore offers the most favorable balance of the three additives.

The relative variation in Jsc between sweep directions falls monotonically from 35.3% in the pristine device to 29.5%, 16.3% and 2.7% for the Tp-, Boc-PDA- and DMTH-modified devices, indicating that photocurrent collection becomes substantially less dependent on scan direction once the additive is present. This is consistent with a lower trap density and reduced interfacial charge buildup [93]. A suppressed contribution from ion-migration-induced polarization is also plausible, although J–V sweeps alone cannot quantify ion motion; impedance spectroscopy or transient measurements would be needed to resolve that contribution directly.
