The observed trend is chemically reasonable. The nitrogen- and oxygen-bearing groups in these additives can coordinate undercoordinated Pb2+ sites or bind charged defects at grain boundaries and interfaces, lowering the density of electronically active traps and curbing non-radiative recombination. The particularly strong effect of DMTH plausibly reflects the arrangement of its hydrazide and methoxy groups, which provide multiple coordination sites within close proximity. We stress, however, that this remains a proposed mechanism: definitive confirmation would require direct spectroscopic or electrical evidence of the passivation interaction.

The reproducibility of the photovoltaic performance was evaluated using 10 independently fabricated devices for each condition (N = 10). As shown in Figure 16, the individual measurements were overlaid on the box plots to provide a direct representation of the device-to-device variation. The statistical values reported in Table 3 were calculated from the same datasets and are presented as the mean ± standard deviation. Figure 16 presents box plots of the solar cells that were examined in this study. The photovoltaic parameters of the pristine and COF-modified devices are presented as box plots. Figure 16a–d display the Voc in V, Jsc in mA cm−2, FF in%, and PCE in% of the solar cells, respectively. The mean Voc increased from 1.142 V for pristine samples to 1.183 V for the DMTH-COF device, a 3.59% increase. The Jsc enhancements are even more substantial, with an increase of 31.09% from 17.53 mA cm−2 for pristine to 22.98 mA cm−2 for the DMTH-COF device. The FF enhancements are also notable, with a pristine value of 73.45% and a DMTH-COF device value of 76.46%, resulting in a 4.10% increase in value. The increase in PCE is even more significant, with a rise from 14.7% for pristine to 20.78% for the DMTH-COF device, resulting in a 41.36% increase. The DMTH-modified devices achieved a mean PCE of 20.78 ± 0.37%, owing to the increases in Jsc, Voc, and FF. The ability of the COFs to passivate defects and improve charge-carrier mobility partially accounts for the increase in Jsc [109]. Furthermore, the best optimal Voc performance for devices is achieved through the reduction in recombination losses following the incorporation of these COFs, aligning with the PL and FTIR observations of decreased non-radiative pathways and improved stability under environmental stress.

To quantitatively link the microstructural evolution induced by COF doping with photovoltaic performance, we correlated the mean grain size extracted from FE-SEM analysis with the Jsc and PCE values obtained from J–V measurements. Figure 17 summarizes this relationship for pristine MAPbI3 and for films doped with Tp, Boc-PDA, and DMTH. The x-axis reports the average grain size for each composition (approximately 0.36 µm for pristine, 0.67 µm for Tp-COF, 0.91 µm for Boc-PDA-COF, and 1.00 µm for DMTH-COF), while the left and right y-axes correspond to Jsc and PCE, respectively. Both Jsc (solid green line) and PCE (dotted brown line) increase monotonically as the grain size grows. The pristine film, with the smallest grains, exhibits the lowest Jsc (17.53 mA cm−2) and PCE (14.7%). Introducing Tp-COF leads to moderate grain enlargement and a corresponding increase in Jsc and PCE. Boc-PDA-COF further pushes the grain size close to 0.9 µm and yields a more pronounced rise in both parameters. The DMTH-doped film, which achieves grains near 1.0 µm, delivers the highest Jsc (22.98 mA cm−2) and PCE (20.78%). This trend indicates that enlarging the perovskite grains and reducing the density of grain boundaries are key to improving charge collection and suppressing recombination losses [110]. The correlation in Figure 17 directly supports the microstructure–property–performance linkage established throughout the study. Larger grains formed under COF-assisted crystallization reduce the number of grain boundaries per unit volume, thereby lowering the density of boundary-related traps and non-radiative recombination centers [111]. This structural refinement enables photogenerated carriers to traverse longer distances without recombination, which manifests as increased Jsc and higher internal quantum efficiency. At the device level, this improved collection efficiency, combined with reduced series resistance and higher shunt resistance in COF-doped devices, drives the observed PCE enhancement.

Figure 18 shows the external quantum efficiency (EQE) spectra of PSCs based on pristine MAPbI3 and COF-modified absorbers (Tp, Boc-PDA, and DMTH), recorded under monochromatic illumination in the 300–900 nm range. The pristine device exhibits a maximum EQE of approximately 68% in the visible region (about 400–800 nm), with a pronounced roll-off toward longer wavelengths and an integrated Jsc of around 17.5 mA cm−2, in agreement with the J–V data. The COF-doped devices display progressively higher and broader EQE responses, with the Tp- and Boc-PDA-COF-modified cells already showing enhanced conversion efficiency across most of the spectrum and reduced loss in the red/near-IR region. The DMTH-based device reaches a peak EQE close to 92% and maintains a strong response up to about 800 nm, corresponding to an integrated Jsc of approximately 23.0 mA cm−2.

The evolution of the EQE spectra mirrors the structural and optoelectronic improvements induced by COF incorporation. The higher EQE in the blue–green region reflects more effective photogeneration and collection in the bulk perovskite, consistent with the enlarged grains, reduced microstrain, and improved crystallinity seen in XRD and FE-SEM. The sustained EQE at longer wavelengths for the COF-treated devices, particularly DMTH-COF, indicates that carriers generated deeper in the absorber experience fewer trap-assisted losses and can be extracted more efficiently, in line with the enhanced PL intensity and improved carrier collection inferred for these films. The good agreement between the EQE-integrated Jsc values and those obtained from J–V curves indicates that the COF additives do not introduce significant parasitic absorption or optical losses in the working spectral range. This, together with the enhanced PL and device performance, is consistent with an improvement in internal quantum efficiency through suppressed recombination and optimized charge transport throughout the device stack.

Figure 19 presents a quantitative comparison of the operational stability of pristine and COF-modified MAPbI3 PSCs over 500 h of continuous AM 1.5G illumination (100 mW cm−2) at 25 °C and 50% relative humidity. This accelerated stress test directly probes the susceptibility of the different absorber formulations to photo- and moisture-induced degradation and links the microstructural and interfacial improvements induced by COFs to long-term device performance. The pristine MAPbI3 devices start from Voc = 1.142 V, Jsc = 17.53 mA cm−2, FF = 73.45%, and PCE = 14.7% but deteriorate rapidly under continuous operation. After 500 h, they retain only about 20% of their initial PCE (final PCE ≈ 2.94%). This steep decline is characteristic of unprotected MAPbI3 and can be attributed to the combined effects of moisture ingress and light-induced ion migration [112]. Water molecules diffuse along grain boundaries and interfaces, facilitating hydrolysis of the methylammonium cation, PbI2 segregation, and progressive formation of non-perovskite phases [113]. At the same time, the high density of unpassivated defects at grain boundaries promotes ion migration and interfacial reactions, thereby intensifying non-radiative recombination. These processes manifest macroscopically as a rapid loss of Voc (increased non-radiative losses) and FF (increased series and leakage components), with only modest changes in Jsc as the absorber progressively decomposes.

Incorporation of COFs significantly alters this degradation pathway. DMTH-doped devices, which initially deliver Voc = 1.183 V, Jsc = 22.98 mA cm−2, FF = 76.46%, and PCE = 20.78%, show a noticeably slower performance decay. After 500 h, they retain approximately 50% of their initial PCE, corresponding to a final PCE of approximately 10.39%. The more gradual loss of Voc and FF indicates that DMTH-COF reduces the formation and activation of non-radiative recombination centers during operation. This behavior is consistent with the structural and spectroscopic evidence that DMTH-derived COFs passivate undercoordinated Pb2+ and halide sites through coordination and hydrogen bonding, enlarge grains, and reduce microstrain. The resulting reduction in defect density and ion-migration pathways at grain boundaries delays the onset of moisture-driven decomposition and preserves more of the built-in potential under stress. Devices doped with Boc-PDA-COF also exhibit markedly improved stability relative to pristine cells. Their initial performance (Voc = 1.174 V, Jsc = 21.33 mA cm−2, FF = 75.43%, PCE = 18.88%) translates into a PCE retention of about 41% after 500 h (final PCE ≈ 7.74%). The Boc-PDA protected amine groups in this COF provide a combination of aromatic conjugation and steric protection at the perovskite surface and grain boundaries, which enhances interfacial adhesion, suppresses the evaporation of volatile organic species, and passivates traps. As a result, the evolution of leakage paths and shunt channels is slowed, and the FF remains relatively high even after extended operation. Among the three COF-modified devices. Starting from Voc = 1.152 V, Jsc = 18.75 mA cm−2, FF = 73.54%, and PCE = 15.88%, they maintain approximately 30% of their original PCE after 500 h (final PCE ≈ 4.76%). The relatively superior stability of Tp-containing cells reflects the robust, β-ketoenamine-type network formed by Tp-based COFs, which provides a mechanically and chemically stable framework around perovskite grains. This framework likely enhances lattice rigidity, reduces stress-induced phase transitions, and offers an effective barrier against moisture penetration along grain boundaries. The high PCE retention factor (0.50 at 500 h, compared to 0.20 for pristine) directly evidences this stabilizing effect.

The stability trends across pristine, Tp-, Boc-PDA-, and DMTH-doped devices mirror the way each COF modifies crystallization, defect chemistry, and surface wettability. All three COFs enlarge grains, reduce microstrain, and increase water contact angles relative to pristine MAPbI3, thereby limiting the density of reactive sites and slowing water ingress. At the same time, their distinct functional groups (hydrazide and methoxy in DMTH, Boc-protected amines in Boc-PDA, and keto-enolic motifs in Tp) tailor the balance between passivation strength, lattice rigidity, and interfacial protection. After 500 h, the normalized PCE retention values were approximately 0.20 for pristine MAPbI3, 0.50 for DMTH-COF, 0.41 for Boc-PDA-COF, and 0.30 for Tp-COF. Thus, DMTH-COF produced the highest initial efficiency, whereas Tp-COF provided the highest relative stability under the applied aging conditions. The improved stability of the COF-modified devices is consistent with reduced defect density, modified film microstructure, and increased surface hydrophobicity, although the individual contributions of defect passivation, ion migration, and moisture transport require further direct investigation.

Table 5 compares the photovoltaic performance and stability of the present devices with previously reported COF-modified and additive-engineered perovskite solar cells. The DMTH-containing device achieved a PCE of 20.78%, close to the 20.04% reported for a triazine-based COF additive in MAPbI3 and the 21.35% obtained using MAOCN in the same absorber system. Higher efficiencies have been reported for an amino-functionalized COF in a mixed-cation perovskite (22.13%) and for dual-interface COF modification (24.26%). These values, however, should not be compared solely on the basis of efficiency because the studies differ in absorber composition, device architecture, active area, and measurement conditions. In particular, mixed-cation perovskites generally offer greater compositional flexibility and improved thermal stability compared with conventional MAPbI3.

Among the MAPbI3 devices listed in Table 5, the DMTH-modified cell exhibits the highest open-circuit voltage, reaching 1.183 V compared with 1.04 and 1.126 V in the two most closely related additive studies. This result agrees with the stronger photoluminescence observed for the DMTH-containing film, which suggests that non-radiative recombination was reduced. By contrast, its fill factor of 76.5% remains below the previously reported values of 79.4% and 81.2%. The larger active area used in this work (0.50 cm2) may have contributed to this difference through increased series resistance and current-collection losses, although variations in device architecture and fabrication conditions may also be involved. The stability data must likewise be interpreted in relation to the aging conditions. Most of the reference devices were evaluated during dark storage under ambient or controlled-humidity conditions. In the present study, the devices were exposed to continuous AM1.5G illumination at 50% relative humidity. Continuous illumination can activate degradation processes that are absent or less pronounced during dark storage, including photoinduced ion redistribution, interfacial deterioration, and accelerated decomposition in the presence of moisture. The reported retention values are therefore not directly equivalent. Although the DMTH device does not provide the highest efficiency in the broader comparison, its performance under a more demanding illumination-and-humidity protocol demonstrates the practical value of introducing DMTH directly into the MAPbI3 precursor solution.

This work establishes covalent organic framework (COFs) as a powerful and versatile class of bulk dopants for engineering MAPbI3 perovskite thin films and devices. By integrating three structurally distinct frameworks, DMTH-COF, Boc-PDA-COF and Tp-COF, each prepared from commercially available building blocks, directly into the MAPbI3 precursor solution, we demonstrate that COFs can act simultaneously as crystallization regulators and defect passivators. Unlike most previous reports where COFs are confined to surface passivation layers or used as inert scaffolds, our approach uses COFs as bulk additives to tune film formation and electronic structure in a single solution-processing step, without sacrificing phase purity or process simplicity. Structurally, XRD and FE-SEM show that COF incorporation preserves the tetragonal MAPbI3 phase while driving a profound reorganization of the microstructure. Grain sizes increase from a few hundred nanometers in pristine films to approximately one micrometer in DMTH-modified layers, with concomitant narrowing of diffraction peaks and reduced microstrain. Raman and FTIR analyses reveal that this morphological improvement is underpinned by specific chemical interactions: COF functional groups coordinate undercoordinated Pb2+ sites and participate in hydrogen bonding with MA+ and halides, which relieves local lattice strain, stabilizes the organic sublattice, and suppresses vibrational disorder. These molecular-scale interactions directly reduce the density of electronic traps at grain interiors and boundaries. Optically and electronically, COF doping enhances light harvesting and carrier management without compromising the intrinsic perovskite band structure. Tauc analysis performed with a common background subtraction and a common extrapolation range gives optical bandgaps equal to within 7 meV across all four films at 1.56 eV, consistent with the invariant photoluminescence emission energy and the common EQE absorption onset. Steady-state PL and EQE measurements confirm that COF-treated films exhibit higher radiative efficiency and improved photon-to-current conversion, particularly at longer wavelengths where recombination losses are typically severe. Water contact angle measurements further show that COF doping, especially with DMTH, renders the film surface significantly more hydrophobic, limiting moisture ingress and reinforcing environmental stability at the most vulnerable interfaces. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic comparison of three chemically distinct COFs on MAPbI3, directly correlating COF structure with grain growth, defect passivation, surface wettability, and spectral response within a single, consistent device platform. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy establishes that the framework survives annealing and remains chemically coupled to the perovskite. At the device level, these coupled structural and optoelectronic improvements translate into a clear and statistically robust progression in all key photovoltaic metrics. Relative to pristine MAPbI3 cells, which reach about 14.7% PCE, COF-doped devices exhibit systematically higher Voc, Jsc, FF, and PCE, with the DMTH-based cells achieving Voc = 1.183 ± 0.006 V, Jsc = 22.98 ± 0.46 mA cm−2, FF = 76.46 ± 1.544%, and PCE = 20.78 ± 0.37%. These gains are accompanied by a marked reduction in series resistance and an increase in shunt resistance, reflecting improved grain connectivity, lower trap density, fewer leakage paths, and a more favorable interfacial energy-level alignment inferred from the measured device performance and literature energy levels. Box-plot statistics show that DMTH not only lifts the average performance but also reduces device-to-device variations, which is essential for scalable fabrication. In contrast to more conventional dopants such as simple salts or polymers, the COFs used here deliver concurrent improvements in morphology, energetics, and moisture resistance, highlighting a genuinely multifunctional and previously under-explored design space for perovskite optimization.

Metal halide perovskites have emerged as leading materials for next-generation optoelectronic devices. These materials exhibit exceptional properties, including long carrier diffusion lengths, high absorption coefficients, and tunable band gaps1–4. Currently, solar cell device efficiency has improved substantially. However, a quantitative understanding of charge carrier recombination dynamics remains a key bottleneck for further improving performance and long-term stability5–8.

Photoluminescence (PL) based techniques are important noninvasive techniques for perovskite characterization. Particularly, time-resolved photoluminescence (TrPL) is widely used to probe perovskite carrier lifetimes9–11. TrPL profiles show the luminescence temporal evolution after excitation. Carrier lifetimes are typically extracted from TrPL decay profiles through exponential fitting (\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$I={I}_{0}+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{A}_{i}\exp (-t/{\tau }_{i})$$\end{document}I=I0+∑i=1nAiexp(−t/τi)). However, the multichannel and coupled natures of perovskite kinetics are largely neglected by these phenomenological fitting approaches. Further, carrier lifetimes may vary significantly with measurement conditions. These limitations imply that the extracted lifetimes may lack a clear physical interpretation. On the other hand, differential decay time (\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$${\tau }_{{{{\rm{diff}}}}}\equiv -2{dt}/d{{\mathrm{ln}}}I\left(t\right)$$\end{document}τdiff≡−2dt/dlnIt) is also frequently used to evaluate the carrier lifetime of perovskites. However, Yuan et al. proved that the differential decay time is an ambiguous indicator when represented as a function of time. Plotting the differential decay time as a function of time can obscure quantitative kinetic information because the effective bimolecular recombination coefficient is no longer retained. As a result, important information related to processes such as shallow trap-mediated recombination may be lost. In this case, the analysis mainly preserves the information that the decay follows a power law behavior associated with bimolecular type recombination, while the corresponding recombination coefficient remains inaccessible. In contrast, plotting differential decay time against quasi-Fermi-level splitting or carrier density can retain meaningful recombination information12. Accordingly, perovskite recombination kinetics may be obscured when they are interpreted solely using lifetimes derived from exponential fitting or differential decay times plotted as a function of time.

In contrast, charge carrier models based on rate equations provide a physical framework for the kinetic interpretation. Through comprehensively considering the temporal evolution of photogenerated species, these models provide a mechanistic description of recombination13–15. Since rate equations consider the initial excitation state, the PL decays under different excitation conditions can be explained mechanistically. However, the application of rate-equation models is limited by two major challenges: (1) the need to predefine the kinetic model based on a limited set of experimental observations, which can lead to poorly constrained parameter estimation; and (2) parameter non-uniqueness arising from strong coupling among multiple recombination channels. Specifically, the same TrPL decay can be reproduced by several distinct parameter sets.

Recent data-driven strategies offer promising alternatives16–20. For example, Bayesian inference has been adopted to invert kinetic behaviors in several semiconductors21–23. However, Bayesian inference often incurs substantial computational overhead because it requires a large number of forward simulations. In contrast, deep learning (DL) provides a more computationally economical and efficient data-driven approach. In materials science, DL has been employed in crystal structure prediction, phase classification, and spectroscopy analysis24–26. By establishing mappings from TrPL profiles to kinetic parameters, it can provide direct physical kinetic solutions quickly. Once trained, the DL model can rapidly predict kinetic parameters without repeated optimization. Lee’s group has conducted in-depth research on determining organic light-emitting-diode electroexcitation kinetics by DL. They successfully extracted coefficients of the polaron recombination and the triplet-triplet annihilation from the time-resolved electroluminescence27,28. While fairly high accuracy has been achieved, the model output is limited to a single kinetic parameter. To date, developing a single model capable of predicting multiple kinetic parameters remains largely unexplored.

In this work, we show that TrPL decay profiles alone are insufficient to uniquely determine carrier kinetics in perovskites. This is due to the existence of non-unique solutions. We demonstrate that incorporating excitation-dependent PLQY provides an orthogonal constraint that greatly alleviates parameter non-uniqueness. Previous work has shown that the curves of PLQY as a function of excitation pulse energy and repetition frequency help to verify the validity of the kinetic model29. This may be attributed to the fact that PLQY adds an independent steady-state constraint to the ratio between radiative and nonradiative recombination channels. Recently, using an analytical method, Hüpkes et al. demonstrated that trap depth significantly affects the steady-state PLQY and transient PL responses of halide perovskites30. Although analytical treatments are essential for understanding limiting cases, they usually rely on simplified assumptions and cannot easily resolve the fully coupled nonlinear kinetics. The community still needs an efficient and scalable solution for extracting multiple coupled kinetic parameters. Building on this insight, we develop a DL-based framework that jointly analyzes TrPL and PLQY data. The proposed framework is able to directly extract physically meaningful kinetic parameters (Fig. 1a).Fig. 1Schematic diagram of the present work and the kinetic model.a Schematic diagram of the present work: leveraging AI to extract perovskite charge carrier kinetics from TrPL+PLQY joint characterization. b Schematic diagram of the kinetic model incorporating trap states with the following processes: ① bimolecular recombination, ② electron capture, ③ hole capture, ④ electron emission, and ⑤ Auger recombination. c Influences of kinetic parameters on normalized TrPL decay profiles (five simulated cases). d Enlarged view of simulated cases 1 and 2, where TrPL decay profiles almost overlapped. e Influences of kinetic parameters on PLQY as a function of photocarrier generation rate. f A detailed comparison of simulated cases 1 and 2.

Here, we construct a large training pool capturing diverse kinetic scenarios by high-throughput TrPL and PLQY simulation. A DL framework is designed to extract six key kinetic parameters, namely, effective external band-to-band bimolecular recombination coefficient γeh, electron capture coefficient γec, hole capture coefficient γhc, trap density NT, electron emission coefficient γee and Auger recombination coefficient γAug. The finalized DL model achieves high accuracy across target parameters, with all coefficients of determination (R2s) over 0.9. The model is adopted to predict kinetics for four deposited perovskite films. The high prediction accuracy is confirmed after comparison with the experimentally fitted parameters. The device-level electrical characterizations further show trends consistent with the DL-predicted kinetics. Together, this work establishes a general and robust data-driven framework for quantitative analysis of kinetics in perovskite semiconductors.

paragraphs.section: Kinetic model and non-uniqueness of TrPL analysis
paragraphs.text: To comprehensively capture coupled processes, the electron trap states are incorporated into the kinetic model, see Fig. 1b35. Following the conventional Shockley–Read–Hall terminology, the trap-mediated processes considered here are electron capture, hole capture, and electron emission36. To limit the number of unknown kinetic parameters, we assume an electron trap located above the intrinsic level and closer to the conduction band, for which hole emission is much weaker than electron emission. The hole emission is therefore neglected in the present kinetic model. Upon photoexcitation, the photogenerated species undergo multiple competing pathways, including ① direct band-to-band bimolecular recombination, ② electron trapping (electron capture), ③ nonradiative recombination of trapped electrons with valence band holes (hole capture), and ④ electron emission from traps. The TrPL decay profiles differ substantially under different excitation fluences. At low excitation fluence, the curve tends to an exponential decay dominated by monomolecular recombination; at high excitation fluence, the curve tends to a power law decay dominated by bimolecular recombination. This is due to the existence of trap states. When the density of photogenerated carriers is lower than the density of trap states, free electrons or holes preferentially undergo trap-mediated monomolecular recombination with trap states. When there is a high concentration of charge carriers, free charge carriers that fail to fill trap states undergo bimolecular recombination. Trap-related processes are dynamic processes involving capture and emission.

paragraphs.section: Kinetic model and non-uniqueness of TrPL analysis
paragraphs.text: At high carrier density conditions, on the other hand, higher-order processes such as third-order Auger recombination may also contribute to excited state dynamics. This mechanism typically manifests as anomalous signatures, such as high-fluence roll-off in PLQY and super-linear early-time TrPL behavior. ⑤ Auger recombination is thus incorporated in the present model via the term γAugnenh(ne+nh). Considering the low exciton binding energy (typically within the range of 2–55 meV) of perovskites, which is comparable to thermal energy (\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$${k}_{B}T\cong$$\end{document}kBT≅2 meV at room temperature), excitons tend to dissociate rapidly, and their equilibrium population is generally negligible compared with the total excited state density37–39. Consequently, the contribution of excitons is not considered. Therefore, the interpretation of excitation-density-dependent photo physics is restricted to regimes predominantly governed by monomolecular, bimolecular, and trimolecular processes involving photogenerated charges and traps.

paragraphs.text: In fact, excitation-dependent PLQY in perovskites has been extensively investigated. deQuilettes et al. reported a pronounced excitation intensity dependence of PLQY; at high excitation intensities, the PLQY of perovskite can exceed 30%40. paragraphs.section: Kinetic model and non-uniqueness of TrPL analysis
paragraphs.text: To gain more insights into the physical impact of kinetic coefficients on experimental observations, we simulated the trends of TrPL and PLQY with increasing kinetic coefficients. Figure 2a–c illustrates the changes with gradually increasing trap densities. Overall, the TrPL decay becomes progressively faster as NT increases. The influence is relatively weak at low NT but becomes pronounced at higher trap densities. Increasing NT suppresses the rise in PLQY. This is because traps become increasingly difficult to fill. A higher photogenerated carrier generation rate is required to fill the traps to achieve recombination luminescence. Notably, PLQY provides a clearer picture compared to the weak trend of TrPL at low trap densities. The changes with the γee are shown in Fig. 2d–f. Unfortunately, even when the γee span two orders of magnitude, changes in TrPL remain almost imperceptible. This suggests that electron emission information extracted solely from TrPL may be unreliable. However, electron emission dominates carrier dynamics over long timescales, making its accurate extraction crucial41. By contrast, it can be seen that at low carrier generation rates (1020–1021 cm−3 s−1), PLQY can provide relatively clear distinctions, providing improved sensitivity for extracting the γees. The same issue arises with the γAug; Auger recombination has a small effect on TrPL decay (see Fig. 2g). This effect may be enhanced under extremely high photoexcitation. Fortunately, Auger recombination has a significant effect on PLQY at high photogeneration rates (Fig. 2i). As the γAug increases, the peak value of PLQY tends to decrease. This reflects the gradual dominance of Auger recombination. paragraphs.section: Deep learning framework for kinetic parameter extraction
paragraphs.text: Based on the introduced physical insights, we developed a supervised DL framework to directly extract kinetic parameters from the joint TrPL + PLQY profiles, as illustrated in Fig. 3a. The initial photogenerated charge carrier density (N0) is included to enable the model to account for different excitation states42. First, six key parameters (γeh, γec, γhc, NT, γee, γAug), together with the initial carrier density N0, were randomly sampled within physically reasonable ranges, which are listed in Supplementary Table 2. A total of 200,000 parameter sets were finally generated. From the distribution histograms of the generated parameters in Supplementary Fig. 2, it can be seen that the parameter data points are evenly distributed within the sampling ranges. For each parameter set, TrPL decay profiles and PLQY curves were simulated by solving the kinetic model. The acquired TrPL profiles then undergo a preprocessing procedure that limits the profiles to a reasonable time window and decay cutoff. Afterward, the learning pool was constructed by pairing the processed profiles with their associated kinetic parameters. Curve diagrams are plotted in Supplementary Fig. 3 using 10,000 randomly selected simulation cases. paragraphs.section: Deep learning framework for kinetic parameter extraction
paragraphs.text: The DL model is used to map the input PL data and associated N0 to the six kinetic parameters. An optimization procedure is performed, which aims to explore the accuracy boundaries with the appropriate sample size, number of sampling points, and the neural network architecture. The DL optimization process is introduced in the Supplementary Note 2, Supplementary Figs. 4, 5, and Supplementary Tables 3, 4. Finally, 200,000 entries and 200 sampling points per profile (a 200,000 × 200 matrix) are determined. The final input comprises 200 TrPL points, 200 PLQY points, and one initial carrier density value, yielding 401 input features per sample. The neural network architecture was determined as 401:1800:1800:6 with a dropout rate of 0.048, as illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 6. The models were implemented in Python 3.12.7 (PyTorch). According to FAIR principles, the complete database, trained model package and code are provided, see data availability statement43.

paragraphs.section: Deep learning framework for kinetic parameter extraction
paragraphs.text: From the R2 bar cluster of the model trained solely on TrPL profiles, poor modeling performance on all kinetic parameters except for the γeh (R2 = 0.86) is observed. Particularly low accuracy is observed for Auger recombination, with R2 of 0.057. Meanwhile, the model trained only on PLQY data suffers from limited performance, with the R2 range of 0.64–0.83. The reason for the insufficient accuracy is that the parameters are obtained by solving the kinetic models under steady-state conditions, leading to a lack of interpretation of the instantaneous PL. In contrast, the model trained on TrPL + PLQY joint data yields R2s ranging from 0.76 to 0.94. The improvements in R2s imply that TrPL and PLQY provide each other with orthogonal information to make accurate inferences. After optimization, R2s of all target parameters are further boosted above 0.9. From the correlation scatter distributions of the optimized model in Fig. 3c, most scatters lie close to the identity line, showing good agreement between the predicted and labeled values. The above results indicate that independent TrPL or PLQY characterizations are insufficient to provide adequate kinetic information. The combined characterization strategy is more effective for extracting the full set of kinetic parameters than either dataset alone. Furthermore, we train the model using TrPL data with added experimental noise to explore its predictive ability on real experimental data. Fortunately, except for the test R2 for the γee, which decreased to 0.73, the R2s for all other coefficients are above 0.84, demonstrating that the model remains reasonably robust to the level of simulated experimental noise. The predictive scatter plot is included in Supplementary Fig. 7. To further examine the extensibility of the proposed framework, we additionally applied it to a more complex ETL half device architecture, glass/FTO/SnO2/perovskite, in which electron extraction and interfacial nonradiative recombination introduce additional kinetic pathways beyond bulk carrier recombination. The corresponding kinetic model, parameter ranges, and DL prediction performance are provided in Supplementary Note 3 and Supplementary Figs. 8, 9.

In studies involving TrPL measurements of perovskite films, the temporal acquisition windows and PL decay cutoffs vary. Despite the widespread use of TrPL as a diagnostic tool, a community-wide standardized protocol for excitation conditions and data analysis is still lacking. Consequently, reported carrier lifetimes and recombination parameters often depend strongly on the selected measurement window and fitting methodology, rather than reflecting intrinsic material properties51,52.

Here, we trained models using different time windows and different decay cutoffs. It is determined that a time window of 2 µs and a decay cutoff of 0.01 provide sufficient kinetic information. This setting applies to the N0 in the range of 1015–1017 cm−3, which corresponds to the excitation fluence range of 100–2000 nJ cm−2 in our model cases (500 nm thick polycrystalline film with absorption coefficient of 105 cm−1 at 532 nm wavelength). The criterion is not universal. For high-quality single crystals, 2D perovskites, and nanocrystals, we recommend using our proposed methodology to train their proprietary models. Further reductions in either the time window or the decay cutoff lead to a pronounced decrease in prediction accuracy, indicating the loss of critical kinetic information. Therefore, TrPL measurements employing a 2 μs time window and a cutoff of at least 0.01 are identified as a practical and reliable condition for AI-assisted kinetic analysis. This conclusion is further confirmed by the area retention analysis of the area under TrPL decay, where both the time window and the cutoff window retain more than 95% of the area information. A detailed discussion is provided in Supplementary Note 5, Supplementary Figs. 21 and 22.

Combined with the initial photogenerated charge carrier density in TrPL (N0), the measured TrPL and PLQY profiles were imported to the trained DL model. To verify the accuracy of the model, the experimentally fitted (genetic algorithm) parameters and the DL-predicted parameters are presented in Fig. 6, and their numerical values are summarized in Supplementary Table 6. It can be seen that the model provides highly accurate predictions for the studied kinetic parameters. Figure 6a shows the comparison results of the bimolecular recombination coefficients. The strong agreement between the experimental and predicted values suggests the model can effectively identify changes in band-to-band radiative recombination behavior caused by compositional engineering and passivation treatment. The γehs of the passivated perovskites are all improved (1.87 × 10−11 cm3 s−1 to 2.65 × 10−11 cm3 s−1 in CsFAMA, 2.72 × 10−11 cm3 s−1 to 3.61 × 10−11 cm3 s−1 in FAMA), which is consistent with the enhanced radiative recombination observed after passivation.

The comparison of trap-related kinetics is shown in Fig. 6b–e. The electron capture and hole capture processes are reasonably reproduced, as shown in Fig. 6b, c. Since these two parameters are directly related to carrier trapping and trap-assisted nonradiative recombination pathways, the agreement confirms that the model is sensitive to trap-mediated kinetic processes. Both coefficients decrease through passivation. The decrease in the γhc indicates the suppression of nonradiative recombination. Although the γec is not directly related to nonradiative recombination, its decrease reduces the probability of trap-assisted nonradiative recombination. NT is a key indicator of trap density in perovskite films. The Fig. 6d suggests that the model can distinguish differences in trap densities among the studied films. Compared to experimental values, the parameters predicted by DL clearly show the difference in trap density before and after passivation (CsFAMA reduced from 7.35 × 1015 cm−3 to 6.05 × 1015 cm−3, and FAMA reduced from 7.31 × 1015 cm−3 to 4.88 × 1015 cm−3). This is attributed to the model’s generalizable judgment based on large-scale data. In Fig. 6e, the γee is well predicted, indicating that the reverse release of trapped carriers back to the free carrier population is captured by the model. This is essential for describing delayed recombination and long tail features in TrPL decay curves. In general, differences in perovskite compositions have little effect on electron emission, while passivation slightly increases the probability of it.

Although Auger recombination typically becomes significant at high carrier concentrations, the DL model exhibits high predictive sensitivity for the γAug and preserves the relative differences among the four films, see Fig. 6f. This demonstrates the model’s effectiveness in extracting higher-order recombination information. The predicted Auger recombination coefficients are lower for the passivated films, indicating a reduced intrinsic tendency toward Auger recombination within the investigated model.

The kinetic parameters of the samples under 3000 nJ cm−2 fluence excitation in TrPL measurements were further predicted using the DL model, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 23. Although the carrier concentration generated by 3000 nJ cm−2 fluence excitation exceeds the modeling range of DL, the model still achieved fairly high accuracy. This result suggests a degree of robustness beyond the training range under the present experimental conditions.

paragraphs.section: Kinetic evolution reconstructed from DL prediction
paragraphs.text: To further examine whether the DL-predicted parameters can provide physically meaningful information, we reconstruct the charge carrier kinetics in transient and steady-state recombination processes of four investigated film samples. As illustrated by Fig. 7, the reconstructed kinetic evolution reveals distinct charge carrier recombination, capture, and release behaviors of different films.Fig. 7Reconstructed carrier kinetics after photoexcitation of FA0.9MA0.1PbI2.85Br0.15 (FAMA), passivated FA0.9MA0.1PbI2.85Br0.15 (Passivated FAMA), Cs0.05FA0.90MA0.05PbI2.85Br0.15 (CsFAMA), and passivated Cs0.05FA0.90MA0.05PbI2.85Br0.15 (Passivated CsFAMA) samples based on DL predicted parameters.a Filled trap density (nT) as a function of time. b Cumulative carriers consumed by bimolecular electron–hole recombination. c Cumulative carriers consumed by hole capture. d Instantaneous bimolecular recombination rate (γehnenh). e Instantaneous trap-assisted hole capture rate (γhcnTnh). f Steady-state carrier concentration as a function of generation rate. g Trapped carrier concentration (nT) as a function of carrier concentration. h Trap-assisted hole capture rate (γhcnTnh) as a function of trapped carrier concentration.

paragraphs.section: Kinetic evolution reconstructed from DL prediction
paragraphs.text: Figure 7a shows the evolution of the filled trap density nT after pulsed photoexcitation in TrPL. The filled-trap densities of all samples increase rapidly at the initial time. This is because free carriers are captured by empty trap states through the electron capture process. After reaching the maximum value, nT gradually decreases. This decrease is caused by the carrier removal through the trap-assisted hole capture and electron emission processes. The different values and decay trends reflect the competition between electron capture and emission. Specifically, the passivated samples exhibit lower filled trap populations, consistent with reduced involvement of trap-mediated pathways under the investigated conditions. This observation agrees with the expected role of passivation in suppressing trap-mediated carrier loss.

paragraphs.section: Kinetic evolution reconstructed from DL prediction
paragraphs.text: Using bimolecular electron-hole recombination and hole capture as examples, we show the consumption of accumulated carriers in Fig. 7b, c. These two cumulative carrier loss channels can directly explain the redistribution of carrier recombination pathways between radiative and trap-assisted nonradiative channels. The cumulative number of carriers consumed by radiative recombination increases with time and gradually approaches saturation as the free carrier density decreases. Under the same excitation conditions, a larger cumulative radiative contribution indicates that a greater fraction of photogenerated carriers undergoes radiative rather than trap-assisted nonradiative recombination. This behavior is indicative of improved optoelectronic quality, because the effective radiative recombination is closely associated with higher PLQY and lower nonradiative voltage loss in perovskite absorbers. In contrast, the cumulative number of carriers consumed through hole capture corresponds to the trap-mediated nonradiative recombination term. The cumulative hole capture curves represent clear differences among the four films, demonstrating that trap-related loss is largely influenced by material composition and passivation. Lower cumulative hole capture contributions are favorable for longer carrier lifetime and higher luminescence efficiency.

paragraphs.section: Kinetic evolution reconstructed from DL prediction
paragraphs.text: The instantaneous kinetics further clarify the temporal origin of these differences. As illustrated in Fig. 7d, the bimolecular recombination rate rapidly reaches a maximum after excitation, then decreases rapidly with time. Such behavior is expected for a second-order recombination process, in which the rate is proportional to the product of electron and hole concentrations. Consequently, when the carrier density is high, the bimolecular recombination dominates the early stage of the TrPL decay. In comparison, the hole capture rates show a different temporal behavior, which reaches its maximum rapidly and then decreases more slowly (Fig. 7e). This is because it depends not only on the free-carrier density but also on the instantaneous trap filling. Therefore, the trap-mediated processes become increasingly important at the late decay stage, especially when the trapped carriers still exist after the free carrier density has decreased. Under the same excitation condition, the passivated film shows a larger radiative contribution and a smaller trap-assisted hole capture contribution, consistent with reduced nonradiative loss.

paragraphs.section: Kinetic evolution reconstructed from DL prediction
paragraphs.text: The cumulative carrier consumptions and instantaneous consumption rates for all kinetic pathways are shown in Supplementary Figs. 24 and 25. Overall, bimolecular recombination and trap-mediated hole capture remain on the same order of magnitude over time, but bimolecular recombination is larger. In contrast, Auger recombination is an order of magnitude smaller. Therefore, at a fluence of 1000 nJ cm⁻2, bimolecular recombination within the perovskite film dominates, followed by trap-mediated recombination, with Auger recombination being much weaker.

paragraphs.section: Kinetic evolution reconstructed from DL prediction
paragraphs.text: We further performed kinetic calculations under steady-state excitation. The charge carrier concentration increases with the generation rate. However, the two do not simply follow a linear relationship, but are regulated by a balance among radiative recombination, trap-mediated recombination, and Auger recombination. We note that, in general, passivated samples sustain higher steady-state carrier concentrations (Fig. 7f). The carrier concentration begins to increase markedly when G exceeds approximately 1021 cm−3 s−1. paragraphs.section: Kinetic evolution reconstructed from DL prediction
paragraphs.text: The passivated samples exhibit higher filled trap densities because their higher steady-state free carrier densities increase the electron capture flux, despite their lower total trap densities and capture coefficients. As we stated earlier, electron capture only indicates the probability of trap-mediated nonradiative recombination to a certain extent; specific kinetic insights can only be obtained by analyzing specific process channels. Taking the hole capture rate as an example, Fig. 7h shows its evolution with filled trap density. As the filled-trap density increases, the trap-assisted hole capture rate becomes progressively larger with increasing nT, confirming that the filled-trap density affects the intensity of trap-mediated nonradiative recombination. Compared to the control group, at a specific filled trap density, the hole capture rates of the passivated films are lower. Moreover, the passivated films reach a comparable hole-capture rate only at a higher filled trap density. The complete steady-state kinetic pathways of the studied samples under steady-state excitation are shown in Supplementary Fig. 26.

paragraphs.section: Kinetic evolution reconstructed from DL prediction
paragraphs.text: In brief, our proposed method for resolving carrier dynamics using DL achieves high accuracy. The reconstructed kinetic evolution indicates that the DL-predicted parameters lead to physically consistent carrier dynamics. Compared with conventional fitting methods, this method exhibits several advantages: (1) It provides a deterministic parameter prediction for each input profile within the trained parameter space; (2) It reduces the data processing time requirement from tens of minutes to microseconds; (3) It allows batch data processing; (4) No large scale parallel computing is required, model training can be completed in hours on a local workstation (AMD Ryzen 7 5800H CPU, 16 GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 GPU); (5) Once trained, the packaged model can be repeatedly applied to new datasets acquired under conditions consistent with the training domain, without retraining for each individual sample. Systematic comparison workflows between conventional fitting and the DL methods are provided in Supplementary Fig. 27.

paragraphs.section: Kinetic evolution reconstructed from DL prediction
paragraphs.text: In summary, we present a deep learning (DL) based framework for quantitatively extracting charge carrier recombination kinetics in metal halide perovskites using combined time-resolved photoluminescence (TrPL) and photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) measurements. We show that TrPL decay alone suffers from intrinsic parameter non-uniqueness, whereas excitation-dependent PLQY provides a critical complementary constraint. This complementary steady-state constraint enables more physically meaningful parameter determination while substantially alleviating parameter non-uniqueness.

paragraphs.section: Kinetic evolution reconstructed from DL prediction
paragraphs.text: Based on physically grounded rate equations, we generated a high-throughput dataset comprising 200,000 paired TrPL and PLQY profiles. The optimized DL model achieves excellent predictive accuracy, with R2 values exceeding 0.9 for all six kinetic parameters (γeh, γec, γhc, NT, γee, and γAug) across multiple orders of magnitude. Experimental studies of FA0.9MA0.1PbI2.85Br0.15, Cs0.05FA0.90MA0.05PbI2.85Br0.15, and samples passivated with 4-MeO-PEAI further validate the approach. The extracted kinetics show strong agreement with experimental fitting results, confirming the reliability of the framework. Independent optical and electrical measurements further provide qualitative support.

paragraphs.section: Kinetic evolution reconstructed from DL prediction
paragraphs.text: After introducing PLQY, we identify an appropriate TrPL acquisition window, namely a time range of 0–2 μs and a normalized TrPL intensity range of 1–0.01, for excitation fluences spanning 100–2000 nJ cm−2. This guideline provides a practical basis for standardized TrPL measurement protocols.

paragraphs.section: Kinetic evolution reconstructed from DL prediction
paragraphs.text: More broadly, this work establishes DL as a powerful tool for data-driven kinetic analysis in semiconductors. Future work may incorporate physics-informed constraints, such as range constraint losses and kinetic consistency losses, to improve physical interpretability and generalization. However, a balance needs to be struck between model performance and computational cost. The framework may be extendable to other semiconductor systems, such as low-dimensional perovskites, colloidal quantum dots, direct bandgap III–V and II–VI semiconductors, and organic emissive semiconductors. Future integration with imaging-based models may enable direct extraction of kinetic mechanisms from spatially resolved characterization data.

Microscope slides were sonicated sequentially with 2 vol% Hellmanex in DI water, DI water, acetone, EtOH for 15 min each, and finally irradiated under UV-ozone for 40 min to remove the last traces of organic residues. Unless otherwise specified, precursor preparation was performed in an argon filled glovebox. 1.6 M FA0.9MA0.1PbI2.85Br0.15 perovskite precursor solution was prepared by dissolving 0.262 g FAI, 0.009 g MABr, 0.723 g PbI2 (3% excess in mol), 0.029 g PbBr2, 0.035 g MACl (as additive) in 1 mL DMF/DMSO (8:2, v/v) solution. 1.6 M Cs0.05FA0.90MA0.05PbI2.85Br0.15 perovskite precursor solution was prepared by dissolving 0.021 g CsI, 0.249 g FAI, 0.009 g MABr, 0.760 g PbI2 (3% excess in mol), 0.029 g PbBr2, 0.035 g MACl (as additive) in 1 mL DMF/DMSO (8:2, v/v) solution. Passivation solution was prepared by dissolving 3 mg of 4-MeO-PEAI in 1 mL of IPA. The precursor and passivation solutions were then transferred to a dry room with a controlled humidity lower than 20% and stirred for 40 min and 60 min. After filtration through a 0.2 μm polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) filter, 40 μL of the precursor solution was deposited on the microscope slide. After the precursor was spread on the surface, the solution was spin coated at a speed of 5000 rpm for 25 s, with an acceleration of 2000 rpm/s. At 19 s after the start of spin coating, 500 μL of anisole was continuously dispensed onto the center of the spinning substrate over approximately 1 s. After that, the substrates were moved to a hotplate at 100 °C and kept for 30 min. For passivated samples, 40 μL of passivation solution was dynamically spin-coated on the cooled perovskite film after filtration through the 0.2 μm pore size PTFE filter, without annealing.

2 × 2 cm2 FTO substrate glasses were etched by an acid solution (HCl: DI = 2: 1, v/v) and zinc powder as an etchant in a 2 × 0.4 cm2 side area. The etched area was covered with zinc powder first and followed by dropwise addition of the acid solution. The unetched area was protected by PTFE tape. After etching, the PTFE tape was removed and the substrates were cleaned by DI water. Before spin coating the electron transport layer (ETL), substrates were sonicated sequentially with 2 vol% Hellmanex in DI water, DI water, acetone, EtOH for 15 min each, and finally irradiated under UV-ozone for 40 min to remove the last traces of organic residues. The ETL material was prepared by adding 10 mM KCl into a solution with a volume ratio SnO2: DI water = 1:3. After stirring for 30 min and filtration through a 0.2 μm pore size polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) filter, the ETL solution was spin-coated on the substrates at 3000 rpm for 30 s with an acceleration rate of 1000 rpm/s. Next, a 2 × 0.5 cm2 area of the SnO2 film (opposite the etched area) was wiped off with a cotton swab dipped in DI water. Then the substrates were annealed at 100 °C for 10 min and moved to the dry room. Before depositing the perovskite layer, the substrates were irradiated under UV-ozone for 20 min. The perovskite precursor preparation and film deposition procedures were identical to those described in the “Film deposition” section. The hole transport layer (HTL) solution was prepared by mixing 0.090 g spiro-OMeTAD, 36 µL tBP, 23 µL of Li-TFSI solution (520 mg/mL in acetonitrile) with 1 mL CB in the argon glove box. Then the HTL solution was transferred to the dry room and stirred for 1 h. After filtration through a 0.2 μm pore size PTFE filter, 40 µL of the solution was dynamically spin coated on the surface at 4000 rpm for 30 s with an acceleration rate of 1000 rpm/s. Next, the same 2 × 0.5 cm2 area of the perovskite film and the HTL was wiped off with a cotton swab dipped in 2ME. The prepared samples were stored in the dry room for 2 days for oxidation. Finally, 80 nm of silver as the electrode was thermally evaporated on the HTL layer at a rate of 2 Å/s under a base pressure of approximately 10−6 Torr.

The J–V characteristics of the as-prepared solar cells were measured using a solar simulator (Newport Oriel Solar 3 A Class AAA, 64023 A) and potentiostat (CHI 660D, CH instruments) under 1 sun illumination of the AM 1.5 G spectrum (100 mW cm−2). The light intensity of the solar simulator was calibrated using a standard Si-based solar cell (Oriel, VLSI standards) and a light-sensor current controller (Newport Oriel digital exposure controller, Model 68 945). During testing, an antireflective film was attached to the rear side of the glass substrate. The performances of all the devices were measured after covering the active area with a thin mask (0.14 cm2). J–V curves were measured using reverse scanning at a rate of 200 mV s−1 under 1 sun illumination of the simulated AM 1.5 G spectrum (100 mW cm−2) in ambient air (room temperature (≈20 °C) and an RH in the range of 5–10%); all the devices were illuminated under 1 sun for 20–30 s before J–V measurements. SEM images and elemental-content mappings were recorded by a hot-field emission scanning electron microscope (JSM-7600F, JEOL, Japan). XRD patterns of the perovskite films were measured using a D8 Discover instrument with Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.5418 Å). Absorbance spectra were measured using a UV–vis spectrometer (Lambda 45, Perkin Elmer). PL spectra were recorded using a fluorescence lifetime spectrometer (Quantaurus Tau C11367-12, HAMAMATSU) with 464-nm pulsed (10 MHz)-laser (PLP-10, HAMAMATSU) excitation. TrPL decays were measured using a pulsed Nd:YAG laser source (10 Hz) at 532 nm (Surelite, II-10), housed with the Cryogenic Femtosecond Transient Kerr-Gate Spectro-microscopy Facility (NFEC-2025-03-305124). To measure the PLQY, samples were placed in an integrating sphere (Newport, 819C-IS-3.3), and illuminated by a 532 nm continuous wave laser (CNI, MGL-III−532). Optical density filters were used to get low intensities and a focusing lens was placed between laser and sample to get high intensities. An optical fiber coupled to the integrating sphere was used to collect the emitted PL. An IPCE system for photovoltaic measurements in the DC mode with a monochromatic beam generated by a 75-W Xe lamp (USHIO) was used for IPCE spectral measurements.
